6c81546677e5d7f7: Only a handful of NHS trusts are using the cancer app on the controversial £330 million Federated Data Platform (FDP) run by Palantir, while newly released figures raise questions about which trusts are benefiting.
Cancer 360 was designed to bring cancer patients' data from disparate spreadsheets and electronic health records into a central system, helping health professionals prioritize treatment.

Pilots began four years ago, and trusts are not charged directly for the FDP. Yet official figures put Cancer 360's uptake at just five or six trusts. Freedom of Information responses gathered by grassroots campaign group No Palantir in the NHS also reveal discrepancies between reported benefits and recorded use.

In June 2025, NHS England said that Cancer 360 "drastically cut down diagnosis times" and referred to a pilot at Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, which saw the proportion of patients diagnosed within 28 days climb from 72 percent to 85 percent.

The trust began trials in 2022, while working with Palantir under a £23 million contract awarded without competition, before the US firm was awarded the FDP contract in late 2023. Critics argued the FDP procurement was flawed as Palantir had developed use cases under £60 million in non-competitive contracts which were then carried over to the FDP.
Last year, NHS England said Cancer 360 served 46 registered teams and 239 active users, and processed 52,000 patients.

In June 2026, NHS England said there were five trusts using Cancer 360 as of March 2026. Of those, only two were listed as benefiting. In July, health minister Preet Kaur Gill repeated the five-trust usage figure in a Parliamentary answer.

Official data released in October said that as of June, six trusts were using Cancer 360 and five were benefiting, but did not identify the trusts or explain the increase. The stats have since been removed from the NHS England website but are archived here.
In June, NHS England responded to a Freedom of Information request. It said six trusts reported unique users logging into the Cancer 360 app over the last 12 months.

However, two trusts cited as having run successful pilots – Chelsea and Westminster Hospital and Royal United Hospitals Bath – were listed as having zero unique users logging into the system during that period, according to NHS England's reply.
Both trusts were said to have received benefits from the system, according to a FoI response sent to campaign group Foxglove in June this year.
The Register asked both trusts and NHS England to explain the discrepancy.

One of the six trusts said to be logging into the cancer app, East Lancashire Hospitals, reported just one unique user. It later confirmed in an FoI response in August that it was not live with the FDP. It had planned to adopt the platform, leading with Cancer 360, but did not have a date for going live with the app.
No Palantir in the NHS also identified trusts that considered Cancer 360 but decided against adopting it.
East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust considered using the app but rejected it because there was "no immediate requirement for it," according to its FoI response.
In its FoI response, Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said it did not adopt the app because of issues around the metadata requirements.
Meanwhile, official figures on cancer diagnosis waiting times show wider improvements across England. Given Cancer 360's limited uptake, those national gains cannot simply be credited to the app.
In July this year, the UK's statistical regulator told NHS England to ensure ministers are briefed accurately following a row over data used to promote the purported benefits of the Palantir-run FDP.

Campaign group Foxglove had found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live and that Chelsea and Westminster Hospital accounted for 84 percent of the reported fall in outpatient waiting lists, while only 16 trusts were using the FDP tool. The Office for Statistics Regulation began assessing NHS England's claims about the FDP's performance and the quango included more caveats on its website.

Scrutiny of the FDP's reported benefits comes as the government decides whether to continue the Palantir-led contract beyond February 2027. The initial contract was provided for a term of up to seven years, with a maximum value of £330 million.

Reports this week suggest the government is set to renew the contract, but run a parallel procurement to find an alternative to Palantir as pressure mounts to reduce lock-in to a single vendor and boost sovereign technology.

Palantir was founded with startup money from a CIA-linked VC firm and has relied on close ties with the US intelligence, military, and immigration services since its inception, although its recent growth in the wider business market is notable. ®

ca326b32b3ec013a: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature.

Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup, who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself.
The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language.

In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies.

The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay.
Contracts dispute

Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior.
Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel.
Developers have proposed adding Contracts to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults.
But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal (P2900) that made it into C++26.

“The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested, and could be more effectively implemented as a library.

Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig, a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself.

“The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post.

The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adopt Rust. Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language.
Sore losers
Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers.

“Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust."
Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself.

“The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.”
Where to now?

With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”)
ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final.
According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy, the group faces a number of choices.
They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts.
Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology.
Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®
14846866b992fc7d: In Australia, they’re calling it the “Microsoft long weekend” – an outage so pervasive it’s just about made Friday a write-off at organizations which rely on Redmond’s online services, especially Exchange Online.

As The Register reported yesterday, the outage started on Thursday at around 18:00 UTC and saw Microsoft 365 users unable to access email, attend Teams meetings, use cloud PCs, consult Copilot, or enjoy full access to another 15 hosted services.
The software giant says the outage impacts Microsoft 365 services “that interact with Exchange Online and email services.” Services that don’t need Exchange Online remain functional.
The software giant initially blamed the outage on a mysterious “problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”
Microsoft thought it found a fix but quickly admitted “Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.”
In the hours since, the situation has not improved markedly, and Microsoft is still struggling to restore service.
It has also changed the language it uses when discussing the possibility that a cyberattack is the reason for the outage.

As of 04:11 UTC, the company said it could find “no indication this is the result of malicious activity.” An update time-stamped 05:46 UTC stated “As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.”

Microsoft’s status page includes only the company’s most recent update, but its RSS feed preserves each missive. That feed tells a tale of woe that we have distilled into lowlights and present in chronological order:
We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvements where possible in an effort to help support traffic in regions coming online;
We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected;

We’re reviewing traffic flows and affected infrastructure to identify opportunities to optimize routing. This includes verifying the reasons for service failures so we can develop specific actions to improve stability;
We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances;
We're observing partial recovery across regions in which we've applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren't resulting in sustained recovery;

Current actions we are taking include scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce load. However, we are encountering issues with the machines being stuck in a bad state, preventing our changes from syncing as expected.
Microsoft’s latest status update doesn’t suggest this will be over any time soon.

“We’re continuing to pursue multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx and advance the recoverability of the backend servers,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re taking a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure to improve the ability to confirm the developed changes were applied. We’re tracking the results of this approach to verify the servers are showing the anticipated recovery and performance intended.”
Hopefully, Australia and other countries in nearby time zones won’t be the only ones to get an unscheduled long weekend. ®

Updated to add at 2144 UTC Redmond still claims that the situation is in the process of stabilizing with no estimate for when everything might get back to normal. "As infrastructure stabilizes, we're still draining queued messages and rebalancing traffic, so customers may see improved sign-in/access while delivery and processing continue to catch up," it writes on its status page. "We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet. Service access can recover before mail flow fully normalizes." The company issued its latest status update at 2002 UTC and promises another update by Saturday at 0000 UTC.

Updated to add at 1300 UTC Microsoft says it's seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with "broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. We're also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific, although some users may continue to experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation progresses across the remaining affected infrastructure."
Updated to add at 1200 UTC The latest status update at 12:00 PM UTC admits users are still "unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services."
d9dc5db21bdd63b1: Working in tech support can be thankless when gormless colleagues leave you sleepless. Which is why, each Friday, The Register runs a new instalment of On Call – the reader contributed column which ensures your work to keep tech alive doesn't remain unnoticed.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Tim" who told us that while working for a phone company he once rewrote 2,650 lines of C as a six line shell script.
He performed that feat after being asked to fix a data transfer program that, strangely, included a bespoke implementation of the venerable File Transfer Protocol (FTP).
"Writing the script took eight hours, most of it tracking down the source code of FTP so I could see if it would do what I wanted," Tim wrote.

This story took place before the World Wide Web became the way to find information online. To find the code he needed, Tim therefore used a Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) to search remote databases.

"In those days, there was no Linux and AT&T had licensed the Unix source code to universities with the strict proviso that it never be made publicly available," Tim explained. "It took me quite some time using WAIS to track it down – the security could have been better – and read the code."
Having found what he needed, Tim wrote his script, which ran overnight to collect data from the telco's switches, tidied up the raw info, and uploaded it to a mainframe.
"It would automatically page me if it couldn't connect to a switch or mainframe after three attempts," he explained.
The script worked fine, but the telco's networks didn't. Tim's pager was soon going off two or three times a night, every night.
After two weeks of interrupted sleep, Tim's manager kindly told him to give the pager to a colleague.
But that colleague habitually left the pager at work, forgot to turn it on, or conveniently placed it out of earshot.
So Tim reluctantly took back the pager and endured another few weeks of nightly interruptions.
How many consecutive sleepless nights have you endured while On Call? If you have enough energy, click here to send your story with On Call so we can share it on a future Friday. ®

606399e29c9ee7e9: The use of algorithms to design structures has led to new parts optimized for ultralight aircraft, high-bandwidth antennas, and F1 racing cars. But the best algorithmic design techniques still require lots of computation and time: Users only see the final design after it’s complete, after which they often must start the design process all over again to make changes. That process also makes it harder to trust that the final designs are structurally sound. MIT researchers are making algorithmic designs more collaborative with a system that acts like an AI copilot. As the algorithm is generating the structure, it presents regions to the human designer for feedback. In an open-access Communications Engineering paper describing the system, the researchers showed it led to more easily manufacturable structures with higher buckling loads while adding only 15 seconds to the total design time compared to all-algorithmic approaches. The researchers believe the approach, which uses a design technique known as topology optimization, could make algorithmic design more accessible and manufacturable for a broader class of design engineers. “Right now, the human doesn’t have any agency or control over the design process as it’s playing out,” explains lead author Dat Ha PhD ’26, a recent MIT civil and environmental engineering doctoral student who is now a structural designer at LeMessurier. “For these really complex designs, we wanted to also tap into our brain, which is the most complex machine there is, to solve these design problems in a way that’s more practical to industry.” Joining Ha on the paper are Ferdous Alam, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Markus Buehler, the MIT Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor of Engineering; Faez Ahmed, MIT associate professor of mechanical engineering; and senior author Josephine Carstensen, MIT associate professor of civil and environmental engineering. Bringing a human in the loop Topology optimization is one of the most advanced and promising algorithmic design techniques. It uses formal optimization techniques to iteratively fill in the space given for a design in a way that maximally achieves the stated goals. For most applications, the process requires a lot of computation and time. When it’s finally done, the designs can be impractical to build or have other issues the engineer didn’t consider. For instance, some designs might have eight or more beam connections at a single point, which would be difficult to make in the real world. “Engineers are always very skeptical of computer programs, especially if they give you very weird-looking or unexpected designs,” Ha says. “On paper, topology optimization is really powerful and can achieve great, high-performing designs, but its black box nature has made it less widely adopted in industry.” Topology optimization has gotten traction in the automotive and aerospace industries, but it’s been used less to design buildings or bridges, partly because design engineers need to know they can trust the output. “A big limiting factor has been that the design engineer has very little influence over how the design evolves and therefore can’t control undesirable features,” Carstensen explains. “The lack of control and lack of ownership also inhibits its use.” To address those problems, the researchers made topology optimization more collaborative in an approach that Carstensen compares to having a design copilot. Prior attempts at adding human judgment slowed things down dramatically. The researchers’ new system uses machine learning to quickly identify the most likely regions of an algorithmic design that a human would want to change. To train the machine-learning model, the researchers created a synthetic dataset of probable human feedback to thousands of designs that critiqued things like aesthetics, performance criteria, and manufacturability. “We thought if we could create a record of where humans have made changes to these programs, then perhaps there’s a pattern to those choices, which is not very different from other types of machine-learning approaches,” Ha says. Carstensen sees the system as bringing together the best of algorithmic and human design approaches. “The idea is to tap into the brains of the designers and get them to infuse their domain knowledge as the design evolves,” Carstensen says. In demonstrations, the researchers showed their human-in-the-loop approach improved manufacturability and linear buckling load by 39 percent while only modestly increasing the total design time. Right now, the approach only allows users to make structures within identified regions thicker or thinner, but they hope to add other options for modification in future versions. “The hope is that by addressing these hurdles, we open up topology optimization to a much wider audience, not only in industry but also to researchers and students in academia,” Carstensen says. From designs to structures The researchers see their approach complementing AI only-approaches to design. “We are arguing there’s room for both,” Carstensen says. “If you are in a discipline that has a lot of computational resources, you can use the other approach. But if you really need the human input, you can use this collaborative approach.” Adding human input also serves to increase trust. “In some settings, the humans need to make the final decisions before advancing the final design,” Carstensen says. “By involving humans, we can get higher-performing designs to the real world to create higher-performing structures. Because it’s not just about designing good artifacts; it’s about creating good artifacts that humans will actually accept and make.” The work was supported, in part, by the MathWorks Engineering Fellowship Fund, TATA Steel, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium.
666c9ce2ae9f1142: Despite fears about robots replacing humans at work, there are still plenty of things humans can do far better than machines. That’s fine with Robust AI, a startup building robots designed to complement what humans do best. The company’s mobile robot, named Carter, resembles a utility cart on wheels and is designed to fit seamlessly alongside humans in fast-changing warehouse and factory environments. Carter features a force-sensitive handlebar for easy guidance, an AI-powered vision system, and holonomic wheels for instant movement in any direction. As a result, humans can cut Carter off, push and pull it in any direction with one hand, and direct it with gestures or the onboard touch screen. The company’s robots are currently deployed in logistics warehouses and on factory floors, where they help humans while picking or stocking shelves and moving items across facilities autonomously. “In these environments, what really determines success is how the overall system performs,” explains Anthony Jules ’92, SM ’92, who co-founded the company with MIT Professor Emeritus Rodney Brooks. “The robot does some of the work, the people do some of the work, and the backend systems do some of the work. It’s that combination that determines how well your system performs. We believe it’s really important that people have an appropriate level of agency and input so that they’re always moving the system forward.” Collaborative robots Brooks was a faculty member at MIT from 1984 until 2010 and served as the director of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) from 1997 until 2007. While at MIT, he co-founded iRobot, which invented the popular Roomba vacuum and went public in 2005. Later, he co-founded the company Rethink Robotics, which also designed collaborative robots. Jules met Brooks as a graduate student at CSAIL in the 1990s. The two never worked together, but their labs were on the same floor. The pair kept in touch after Jules graduated and co-founded the company Sapient, which went public before being acquired by Publicis in 2015. In 2019, Brooks bumped into Jules at a robotics conference. He told Jules he was thinking of starting a robotics software company, which he compared to a video game engine for training robots. Robust AI was founded later that year. The Covid-19 pandemic caused the founders to shift to creating robots that could autonomously disinfect surfaces, but when it was discovered that Covid-19 was not transmitted via surfaces, they had to pivot again. “That forced us to decide how to use this technology we had been building, which was really about helping robots understand the world more fully,” Jules recalls. “Long story short, I said to Rodney, ‘I have an idea. You’re going to love it and you’re going to hate it. You’re going to love it because it’s solving problems for customers that we’ve been hearing about, and you’re going to hate it because we have to build hardware.” The founders had been interviewing potential customers for years through Robust AI’s early pivots. They finally decided on logistics and manufacturing as the industries to target early on. “When people think about automation in factories, they think about pictures of the 5 percent that are fully automated with $50 to $200 million dollar systems,” says Jules, who now serves as Robust AI’s chief innovation officer. “They don’t think about the vast majority of factories that aren’t automated at all. These factories don’t even have a conveyor belt. They are not going to tear everything out and replace it with a $200 million system.” Robust AI’s robots can be phased into operations as needed and offer several workflows for customers. In one workflow, the robot can guide human workers to specific spaces to retrieve items. In another it can follow humans to important spots for loading. The primary workflows involve Carter robots moving things from one place to another, often in large warehouses or factories, where they say human workers can walk on average 30,000 steps a day. “These are huge spaces, so a person might load the robot with things and then need to bring them to another station, but that could be 400 feet away,” says, Brooks, Robust AI’s chief technology officer. “Now the person can just say ‘done’ and the robot brings it instead. How the robots are integrated into the workspace is entirely up to the customer.” Getting work done Leila Takayama, Robust AI’s vice president of human robot interaction, recently discovered a peer-reviewed study of robots in hospitals, which were used to do things like gather dishes, move sheets, and transport other equipment. The researchers discovered that, in many hospitals, a large number of robots were turned off and against the walls. The nurses said they broke. “What really happened was the nurses were rushing with a patient on a gurney, and the robot sees them in the hallway and stops dead, and they couldn’t get the gurney around them,” Brooks says. “The robots were getting in the way of nurses’ primary tasks.” Robust AI’s approach to technology development is to understand workers’ primary tasks deeply and build features that accelerate those tasks, whether a human or a robot is doing them. “We let humans do what humans are good at in the physical world, which we’ve had millions of years of evolution to get good at, and have the digital system respond to that and provide us with all the things that it is good at,” Brooks explains.

1ea91ef041981ae4: The state deprived a former governor of medical care despite clear warning signs
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Q Company. Fair Use (CC BY 4.0)
Read our special coverage on Venezuela’s fight for democracy and the political crisis that has unfolded since the 2024 presidential elections, after the documented allegations of electoral fraud.

This is the first installment of a series by Luis Carlos Díaz covering cases of torture, neglect, and cruel treatment against political prisoners, based on the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission. Originally published in Runrunes and translated by Caracas Chronicles.

To kick off this series, it is worth examining how the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) on Venezuela was constructed. Based on 213 confidential interviews with 121 victims, relatives, and witnesses, as well as forensic data and judicial documents, the report matches the rigorous evidentiary threshold of “reasonable grounds to believe.”

Despite the Venezuelan state’s complete refusal to cooperate, the FFM’s technical findings expose a crucial reality. Following the United States’ military intervention on January 3 and the capture of Nicolás Maduro, interim president Delcy Rodríguez announced cabinet reshuffles, released hundreds of prisoners, and oversaw a decline in long-term detentions.

However, the United Nations (UN) found that at least 18 high-ranking officials previously implicated in human rights violations and crimes against humanity remain in key positions of power or military command, including Diosdado Cabello, Gustavo González López, Alexander Granko Arteaga, and Vladimir Padrino López. The core architecture of state repression remains fully intact, providing the structural context for the individual cases documented in this series.

Before delving into the case of Alfredo Díaz, I want to address a question that often lingers when we discuss the UN reports: What is all this work actually for? What happens to a report like this once it is published?

The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission was not created on a whim, nor was it meant to issue a general diagnosis and stop there. It was established by the Human Rights Council under Resolution 42/25 in 2019, with a specific mandate: to document the most serious crimes committed in the country to combat impunity, ensure accountability for those responsible, and secure justice for victims. This carries practical consequences, even if they are not immediate.

The FFM is an investigative body, one of only seven active mechanisms of its kind worldwide. That alone underscores how extraordinary our situation is, and how resilient civil society has been in organizing to secure its renewal on four separate occasions. In October, countries in the Human Rights Council voted to extend its mandate for two additional years.

Whenever the FFM concludes there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that an individual participated in a human rights violation, that finding is preserved in secure databases with case files, testimonies, and evidence. This material is not lost, even if no Venezuelan court is willing to use it.

This documentation has already had real effects outside Venezuela. The report notes, for instance, that a federal court in Argentina issued an extradition request in June 2026 against a Spain-based former Venezuelan military officer linked to the 2014 repression. The court relied on the principle of universal jurisdiction — the legal framework allowing a country to prosecute grave international crimes committed elsewhere, when justice is denied in the country of origin. That officer was named in the 2025 special report on the Bolivarian National Guard.

Furthermore, although Venezuela formally denounced the Rome Statute in July 2026 in an attempt to block cooperation with the International Criminal Court, the FFM’s report clarifies a crucial point: a withdrawal from the ICC does not erase or halt ongoing investigations by the tribunal in The Hague for events that occurred while the statute was still in force for the country. In other words, these reports have allowed us to build, fact by fact, the evidentiary record that may one day support a criminal indictment inside or outside Venezuela. This is why more victims and witnesses should be encouraged to share their stories with the FFM.

With that purpose in mind, reading the case of Alfredo Díaz is well worth the effort. Díaz was a former governor of Nueva Esparta and a regional leader of the Acción Democrática party. SEBIN officers arrested him on November 24, 2024, in Ospino, Portuguesa state, leaving his family completely unaware of his whereabouts for four days. This marked the start of multiple due process violations, including incommunicado detention and enforced disappearance. Charged with “incitement to hatred” and “terrorism,” he spent the remainder of his detention unable to appoint defense counsel of his choice or access his own case file.

What makes this case particularly grave, according to the FFM, is not only the arbitrary detention (a serious crime in itself), but what happened to his health. Before his arrest, Díaz had a history of serious medical conditions, including seizures, an anxiety disorder with paranoid traits, and depression. A medical report from that year included pending orders for pharmacological treatment, a CT scan, and a neurological evaluation. The political persecution he suffered rendered him unable to maintain his medical care.

Witnesses who shared a cell with him reported that he suffered at least two severe medical episodes while incarcerated. One occurred in October 2025 and was characterized by intense pain, muscle stiffness, and disorientation, which medical personnel at El Helicoide diagnosed as “indigestion” and a “stomach issue.” No specialist ever evaluated Díaz, the FFM documented, despite repeated pleas from his family and fellow inmates. Such negligence extends the punishment beyond detainees to their loved ones, who remain impotent to help, forced to advocate from a distance.

On December 6, 2025, at around 5:00 a.m. local time, Díaz experienced the same symptoms. His cellmates’ desperate alarms were met with a delayed response. Díaz was eventually transferred to the facility’s medical area, where staff performed resuscitation maneuvers, but he died shortly after at the University Hospital of Caracas. The official cause of death was listed as an acute myocardial infarction.

The FFM is not asserting that Díaz was beaten to death or that a direct order was issued to let him die. Instead, it points to something that is, in many ways, more difficult for state officials to evade: the sustained lack of specialized medical care, despite clear warning signs — repeated for more than a year — was a contributing factor in his death. This constitutes an arbitrary deprivation of life attributable to the state, which inherits a strict obligation to protect the health and life of anyone it takes into custody.

This brings us to the key connection between this case and the core finding mentioned at the start of this series. Díaz was not an isolated case. The FFM also documented the death in custody of Edison José Torres Fernández, a police officer with 24 years of service who was detained for criticizing the government, and whose body bore bruises that went unacknowledged in the official death certificate.

These are distinct stories unfolding within the same detention system and reflecting the same underlying pattern: people incarcerated with known medical conditions left in a coffin, with no one held accountable to date.
Written by Luis Carlos Diaz

1b60a17ac806065d: Angel Bena/PexelsMicrosoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill. According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X, the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”. In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems. This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters. Beyond missed emails or workplace meetings The list of services Microsoft says are “potentially impacted” by the outage is long. It includes services used for email, document sharing, meetings and managing tasks, such as Outlook, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Planner and Microsoft Exchange Online. It also includes Microsoft Defender, a cloud-based cybersecurity service. With so many digital services affected, the real-world impacts of the outage have been widespread, and go far beyond missed emails or workplace meetings. For example, family violence workers reportedly can’t access databases which contain client details. Schools can’t provide online lessons for remote students. Psychologists can’t provide telehealth consultations. Businesses are unable to process orders. Job hunters are unable to make it to planned interviews. Some government service centres have been forced to closed. The disruption also reached services outside Microsoft. OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems with the tools that connect their artificial intelligence (AI) services to Microsoft 365. This shows how a problem in one part of the digital world can affect tools that appear separate, and even services provided by other companies. The outage comes after other disruptions to Microsoft services earlier this year. For example, in January, Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were down for hours. Then in August, Microsoft Outlook and Exchange Online were disrupted by a code update which took several days to fix. A shifting account of what went wrong As of early Friday afternoon Sydney time, Microsoft has not yet named a root cause of the outage, and its account of the failure has shifted since it was first reported. Initially the company said elevated load across multiple regions was reported first. It then clarified the load was not driven by an increase in traffic, but a large number of servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable. Attention then moved to the automated “health checks” Microsoft uses to judge whether a server is fit to carry traffic, and to the component that processes them. The company described a core process on the affected servers as becoming “overwhelmed”. Software deployments and configuration changes were paused while recent changes were reviewed, although none was found to correlate with the start of the disruption. The evidence does not suggest a cyberattack. A distributed denial-of-service attack works by flooding a service with requests from outside until legitimate ones can no longer be answered. Microsoft’s own statement that overall traffic had not increased is difficult to reconcile with that pattern. No evidence of malicious activity has been disclosed, and no group has claimed responsibility. Indeed, Microsoft said: “There’s no indication this is a cyber attack.” The more mundane explanation fits better. Health checks exist to protect a service by withdrawing servers that appear unwell. When the machinery making that judgement is itself at fault, healthy capacity can be removed, and the servers that remain are left to absorb work they were never sized for. Outages of this scale are more often self-inflicted in this way than they are the work of attackers, as the August disruption to Microsoft email by a code update illustrates. Until a post-incident review is published, however, that remains an inference drawn from Microsoft’s own updates rather than a settled account. Microsoft has not yet been able to fix the outage entirely. It says that some of the affected servers are working again, but they “can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic”. Planning for outages like we do for bushfires This outage reinforces the need for all of us to better prepare for digital outages. For individuals, this can involve storing essential information, such as contacts and medical prescriptions, offline in case of an outage. Organisations that rely on one digital provider such as Microsoft or Google for tasks must also prepare back up plans. Crucially, they must also test these back plans to make sure they work in practice and don’t simply exist on paper – similar to how they conduct fire drills and how communities practice bushfire evacuations. As more aspects of our lives become connected – from cars and homes to workplaces, transport and healthcare – and AI becomes more widely used, the consequences of digital disruption may grow. Building resilience must be part of how we plan for that future. e05a2ab3577e9f7c: From Moaz Nair
In any healthy democracy, a vibrant opposition is not a luxury; it is a necessity.
Its role extends far beyond merely opposing the government of the day. It must act as a credible government-in-waiting, offering a distinct, actionable alternative vision for the nation’s progress.
Unfortunately, in contemporary Malaysian politics, the federal opposition — represented by Perikatan Nasional (PN) — is falling drastically short of this democratic mandate.
In the eyes of ordinary citizens, they are increasingly failing to project the image of a responsible, cohesive team capable of governing.
Instead of elevating national discourse, recent parliamentary sessions have frequently devolved into political circuses.
Rather than acting as serious lawmakers, some opposition figures have behaved more like clowns, relying on histrionics, disruptions, and shouting matches to capture headlines.
Consider the chaotic session during the 2026 Supply Bill debate, which descended into an embarrassing shouting match.

The Dewan Rakyat witnessed the unseemly spectacle of opposition members trading insults like “gila” (crazy) and “mabuk” (drunk) with a government backbencher over religious rhetoric concerning alcohol, ultimately leading to an opposition MP being ejected from the august House.
Deficit of substance

The opposition’s core problem lies in a severe deficit of substance. A constructive opposition should serve as a vital check on power by scrutinising legislation, advocating for fiscal discipline, and consistently raising structured concerns regarding governance, transparency, and inflation.

While PN is quick to criticise the current administration’s landmark policy decisions — such as the highly contentious targeted rationalisation of fuel and electricity subsidies and the introduction of digital and carbon taxes — their criticisms often exist in a vacuum.
When civil society and economic think tanks called on PN to present a costed alternative framework to address middle-class cost-of-living pressures, the response was telling.

The opposition leadership flatly dismissed the necessity of drawing up an alternative national budget, calling the exercise “syok sendiri” (self-indulgent) because it would have no chance of being implemented by the current government.
This defeatist stance reveals a fatal misunderstanding of the opposition’s purpose. It is easy to point out a leak in the roof; it is much harder to present the architectural blueprint to fix it.
This lack of policy depth is directly tied to the underutilisation and internal instability of PN’s own structures.

Although the coalition established portfolio committees to function as a shadow cabinet, key leaders have come under heavy fire for failing to drive substantive policy debates or introduce impactful private members’ bills.
The opposition has been sharply criticised for failing to produce a counter-economic blueprint, focusing instead on reactive politics.

Meanwhile, the opposition’s structural credibility took an unprecedented hit when the Registrar of Societies (RoS) cancelled Perikatan Nasional’s registration following fierce infighting between PAS and Bersatu, with top figures in Bersatu publicly blasting the coalition leadership for failing to manage the bloc with democratic principles and transparency.
Over-reliance on identity politics

Compounding this policy vacuum is PN’s over-reliance on identity politics. Analysts have repeatedly noted that the opposition disproportionately prioritises divisive racial and religious rhetoric over concrete economic solutions.
While proponents argue that this positions PN as the champion of a conservative, nationalist vision for Malaysia, this narrow focus inherently alienates the nation’s diverse, multi-ethnic electorate.
A vision built purely on identity cannot resolve currency fluctuations, fix the healthcare system, or improve the quality of education.

Malaysia faces complex global and domestic headwinds that demand rigorous intellectual debate. By choosing rhetorical fireworks over structural alternatives, the federal opposition is letting down the very citizens it aims to represent.

To become a credible alternative government, PN must move past the circus acts, put its shadow cabinet to work, resolve its internal chaos, and prove to Malaysians that they can govern with intellect rather than identity and empty rhetoric.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

7f11750ed4bd7938: Five minutes into a pitch from a former English teacher in 2000, a Japanese tycoon decided he had seen enough and handed him over about US$20 million, roughly RM81 million at today's rates. The tycoon was Masayoshi Son, the teacher was Jack Ma, and by the time Alibaba listed in 2014, CNBC reckoned Son's stake was worth US$50 billion (RM203 billion) or more.
Son's explanation was pure instinct: "It was the look in his eye, it was an 'animal smell'."
That same RM203 billion is what Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says Son now wants to spend here in Malaysia. Let that sink in for a bit.

Speaking in Melaka on Oct 24, Anwar said the SoftBank Group founder had told him over a video call days earlier that he had picked Kuching in Sarawak and sites in Peninsular Malaysia for some US$50 billion of investment. "In what areas? AI, new technology and data centres," Anwar said.
A man who bets big, and sometimes loses big

Son is no stranger to numbers like these. At the height of the dot-com bubble he was, for three days, the richest man on earth, before SoftBank's shares fell 93% by the end of 2000 and, by Bloomberg's tally, some US$70 billion (RM284 billion) of his fortune went up in smoke.

SoftBank later poured billions into WeWork, the office-sharing firm once valued at a whopping US$47 billion (RM191 billion), only to watch it file for bankruptcy in 2023. Yet Son bounced back again, and in June Forbes crowned him Asia's richest person, with US$97 billion (RM394 billion) to his name.
Why Malaysia, and why now?

The answer lies in Son's obsession with artificial superintelligence (ASI), AI that vastly outperforms the brightest humans, which he predicted in 2024 would be 10,000 times smarter than us within a decade. "I think I was born to realise ASI. I am super serious about it," he told shareholders that June.

Superintelligence needs gargantuan amounts of computing power, and computing power needs land, electricity and water. That's why SoftBank has already sunk about US$64.6 billion (RM262 billion) into OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and is planning a US$500 billion (RM2 trillion) data centre campus in Ohio.

Here in Malaysia, he finds what few other countries can offer: RM385.7 billion of data centre-related investment recorded since 2021, according to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA), a government pitching us as neutral, non-aligned ground for technology and, in Sarawak, a state energy company ready to supply the power.

On Oct 8, Son signed a framework agreement with Petroleum Sarawak (Petros) and Grab to explore an AI and digital infrastructure platform in Sarawak. Talk about coming full circle: Grab began life as MyTeksi in Kuala Lumpur in 2012, and SoftBank backed it with US$250 million (RM1 billion) in 2014.
What's in it for you?

The sum is about a tenth of our economy, which the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) put at RM2.03 trillion last year, and more than three times the RM61 billion that Google pledged here on Nov 4.

But here's the thing: data centres are heavy on capital and light on people. The 27 projects approved by the government's Data Centre Task Force, worth RM225.97 billion, are expected to create just 4,053 jobs, or more than RM55 million of investment per job.

Sure, 3,523 of those are high-skilled roles in engineering, networking and cybersecurity, and Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo told Parliament on Oct 28 that Malaysians were expected to fill nearly 90% of them.

I can't help but feel the bigger prize is everything around the servers. Google expects its expansion to support more than 37,000 construction jobs a year but more than 9,000 once the campuses run, and the Sarawak pact lists robotics and local workforce development.
So how do we make sure Malaysians collect on Son's bet? Three things.
1. Get it in writing

SoftBank's only public word so far, an emailed statement reported by Dow Jones, says it is exploring AI and digital infrastructure opportunities with the government and others, but confirms no figure. Nikkei Asia reports it would fund only part of it, with financiers and partners covering the rest.
Putrajaya and Sarawak should publish a phased schedule with dated milestones and SoftBank's own share, so the public can tell a pledge from a project.
2. Make the jobs and contracts Malaysian
The Data Centre Task Force already requires at least 30% local content from approved projects.

For a deal this size, that floor should rise, and SoftBank, which brings robotics and "physical AI" to the Sarawak pact, should train Malaysian technicians there, with MIDA publishing what was being spent locally each year.
3. Make the servers pay for their own power
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Ghani has said data centres on Tenaga Nasional Berhad's (TNB) grid pay market rates without subsidies, and pay for every megawatt they reserve.

Son should go one step further, as Google did when it pledged to add over 1GW of clean energy to the grid without public subsidies, so that no household in Kuching or Klang pays a sen more for his servers.

Son once turned RM81 million and an "animal smell" into a stake worth upwards of RM203 billion. He is now offering Malaysia a bet of the same size, and it's up to Putrajaya to make sure that this time, ordinary Malaysians hold a share of the winnings.

1f15a743e9ad3fdc: While many of us count down to year-end holidays, part of Malaysia anxiously watches the skies. Along the east coast, prolonged monsoon downpours swell rivers and isolate villages. Eastern Johor faces similar dangers.

For city dwellers, the threat is close to home. Flash floods in Kuala Lumpur and the Klang Valley can overwhelm roads within minutes. The patterns differ, but families face the same question: will help reach us when it matters?

The clock began ticking when the northeast monsoon started on Oct 27. The meteorological department forecasts three to five episodes of prolonged heavy rain between November and January. We cannot predict precisely which streets will flood, but we know the season and can prepare.

Repeated flooding can numb us to its seriousness. Yet, it is no mere inconvenience or property problem. People drown, suffer injuries or develop infections after contact with contaminated water. Temporary shelters require safe water, sanitation and infection control. And the damage to health continues beyond the floodwater: a dialysis patient cannot reach treatment, a family loses essential medication, an older person living alone cannot evacuate. Preparedness must protect health as well as homes.
What arrangements does Malaysia already have? Quite a few.
The National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma) coordinates disaster management through national, state and district structures.

Its revised 2024 directive assigns responsibilities to government agencies and sets out how businesses and voluntary organisations can participate. Community-based disaster risk management programmes help residents identify local risks and develop action plans. Rakan Nadma provides a channel for civil society involvement.

These are meaningful foundations. The directive already provides for the district coordination of volunteers and resources, while Nadma's strategic plan seeks better community participation and reporting of NGO activities.
We do not necessarily need another framework. We need to know whether those already in place work when tested.

Imagine a district exercise. Can a local team identify an older resident who needs assistance, organise safe transport, arrange alternative dialysis care and confirm that help has arrived? Counting training certificates or meetings cannot answer that. Emergency medical teams already conduct disaster exercises. Flood scenarios should be a regular, practical part of such training, involving local authorities, healthcare providers and community groups together.

One area deserving particular attention is how we use Malaysia's considerable civil society capacity. During the November 2025 floods in Hat Yai, southern Thailand, Malaysian Sikh humanitarian organisations, volunteer fire brigades and other groups helped with evacuation and relief alongside the authorities.

Malaysia's foreign ministry reported that more than 15 Malaysian groups participated in the wider operation, which evacuated 6,222 stranded Malaysians. That was a collective effort, but it showed what organised citizens can contribute.

We should make it easier for those capabilities to be used here. Before floods, districts should know which organisations have trained boat crews, trucks, kitchens, healthcare teams or storage space. New groups offering assistance need a clear, rapid route to have their capabilities assessed and receive useful assignments. Specialist rescue must remain under trained command. Other volunteers can help with welfare checks, supplies and recovery. All quarters need appropriate communication, protective equipment and clarity about operating costs. Courage is invaluable but it is not a replacement for safety.

Reliable information matters just as much. Previous floods saw relief supplies repeatedly delivered to some evacuation centres while other communities went underserved. The solution is not necessarily another app. Responders need a shared, updated picture of what is needed, what has been offered, who has been assigned and whether assistance arrived. That picture must include families who remain at home, and it must be accessible even when communications are disrupted.

Nor is preparedness solely the federal government's responsibility. Local councils must maintain drains and address known hotspots. Health facilities must test how essential treatment will continue. Businesses can commit transport and storage. Residents' associations can identify neighbours who need help and practise evacuations. Households with the means can prepare medicines, documents and emergency contacts. But shared responsibility does not excuse the government from providing infrastructure, professional rescue services and protection for vulnerable people.
Flood defences remain necessary, even though no drainage system or river barrier can eliminate every risk. Preparing people and services for flooding complements investments in preventing it.
And this is no longer a conversation confined to distant rural districts in Kelantan.

The same questions now face district offices and city councils across the Klang Valley. They, too, must be able to explain which plans have been tested, which organisations can be mobilised, how essential healthcare will continue and what shortcomings were corrected after the last flood.
The measure of preparedness is not simply how much help appears when waters rise. It is how much avoidable suffering we prevent before they do.

1d1cbd202dcbc7c7: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test.
Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday.

Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years.
1a41a8bcb98e2d2e: It might just work.
Manchester United have tried every type of manager. Mauricio Pochettino has tried every type of club.
Two lost souls, who have known better times, meet when past their prime. They have quite a lot in common.
Like two old drunks reminiscing in a bar, both have been through the mill and feel they just haven’t had the breaks.
But together they might just show the world that they can still do it.
Poch wants the job and United want him. Only some cantankerousness from Big Jim can stop it now.

The much-maligned pair of CEO Omar Berrada and Football Director Jason Wilcox deserve credit for going outside the box of bookies’ favourites, Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte, Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann.
They remembered a once-high roller who never quite realised his full potential. And one who always had Fergie’s blessing.
On his part, Poch would not have taken much persuading to leave his USA-sized comfort zone and give the big time one more shot.
When United come calling, you have to be well ensconced at a top club to say ‘no’. When you’re in a retirement village, it’s a no-brainer.
Football is not even among the top four sports in America, so he would never be fully appreciated if he did win something.
And at 54, he’s probably at the optimum age for a football manager. Still young enough to join a kickabout, but old enough to be a father figure.
Crucially, he still has the hunger of a younger man. Despite managing three top clubs – Spurs fans can look away now – his trophies still fit in his carry-on luggage.
All three were with PSG in the so-called farmer’s league and during the Galactico era.
He never managed to crack it with the Neymars and Mbappes, but his greatest frustration was at Spurs, whom he’d transformed thrillingly after being poached from Southampton.
More precisely, he was denied the funds to turn a very good team into title-winners.
Chelsea was the wrong fit and he made a mistake in going there, but the USMNT (US Men’s National Team) was below him.
A warm-hearted, players’ manager, he may click better with United’s disparate youngsters than the emotionless Michael Carrick.
Little did we think the long-haired Argentine defender who ‘tripped’ England’s golden boy Michael Owen in the 2002 World Cup would become so admired in the Premier League.
On television, it looked a clear foul and penalty, which well-positioned referee Pierluigi Collina did not hesitate to give.
David Beckham scored from the spot and England won one-nil.
But Pochettino has always maintained that Owen ‘dived’. It’s not the first time a tall, dark Argentine centre-back has argued about a decision in England’s favour.
The most infamous was skipper Antonio Rattin, who was sent off in the 1966 World Cup quarter-final and refused to leave the field.
It became an international incident that sparked animosity between the two countries well before the Falklands War.
But we have since learned that Poch is no Rattin, who died during the recent World Cup, and Owen is no choirboy.
The Argentinian said of that moment: “When I was managing Southampton, Owen was a TV pundit. I knew he was coming in one day and told my press officer I wanted him to come down and say hello.
“I had the photo ready – the one that clearly shows I didn’t touch him. He signed it and wrote, “You definitely touched me,” along with a smiley face.
“We had a good laugh about it. He was clever, and I was a little bit naive.”
So, apart from a likeable, all-round good guy, what can United fans expect from the latest occupant of one of football’s hottest seats?
He usually needs time, although in his first job at Espanyol, he inspired an amazing turnaround from the relegation zone to tenth in half a season. He even beat Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona!
United would take something similar now, especially if he can conjure up a decent cup run and go deep in the Champions League.
Much may depend on how much cash he can inveigle from the back of Jim Ratcliffe’s sofa.
Having failed to get Daniel Levy to cough up at Spurs, his best bet is to insist on a bundle now while he’s in a position of strength.
Even following from a distance, he must know he’s inheriting the weakest United squad in living memory.
Lying 18th in the table, this season United are averaging just 0.8 points per game. Even the notable flops averaged a point more than that.
All his post-Fergie predecessors – illustrious and not so – had more to work with.
Every United fan is as familiar with the spots as a teenager is with acme, but will the owner respond?
It’s all over the field and, worryingly, even goalie Sanne Lammens is having the heebie-jeebies and he’s considered a rare good buy.
On the other hand, the Old Trafford crowd has shown its ability to rouse the team and a more animated figure in the dugout may help.
That said, Carrick deserves sympathy for the typically shabby way the Ratcliffe regime is treating him.
Asked to carry on as if nothing is happening while the firing squad loads their rifles.
Shocking, but consistent with the INEOS modus operandi in other sports.
The Guardian comments that there’s a Leaving Las Vegas feel to this appointment, and it means the movie, not the casinos.
But given INEOS’s failure rate and Pochettino’s own trophy collection, there’s a Hail Mary element, too.
And when you add that to the firm conviction that nothing will work with the current owners, football is such a contrary sport that you can’t write it off.

c1b8ea1b2fb317cf: Three technologies developed by MIT Lincoln Laboratory are among recipients of 2026 R&D 100 Awards. The awards recognize the 100 most significant innovations that have transitioned to use or been made available for license in the past year. R&D World, an online publication, manages the awards program, which has run annually since 1963. The worldwide competition is judged by an independent panel of science and technology experts and industry professionals. The laboratory's winners overcome obstacles to improving the security and capability of systems. One technology is an operating system designed to protect embedded computers from cyberattacks. Another technology is a platform for integrating superconductor and semiconductor chips in a wafer-scale system for quantum or high-performance computing. The final winner is an algorithm that removes interference 5G base stations incur on co-channel radio frequency (RF) devices.  "These awarded technologies address critical problems in cybersecurity, quantum computing, and communications. We're proud of our dedicated staff who developed and transitioned these technologies for the nation's advantage," says Melissa Choi, Lincoln Laboratory director.  Since 2010, Lincoln Laboratory has received 111 R&D 100 Awards recognizing the transfer of its unclassified technologies to industry and government. Each year, many technology transitions also occur for classified projects. This transfer of technology is central to the laboratory's role as a Department of War (DoW) federally funded research and development center. Secure-by-design operating system Computers embedded in deployed systems — such as satellites, drones, or radars — keep missions intact and people safe. The operating systems (OS) inside these embedded computers, however, are prime targets for cyberattacks. They are large, complex, and built on decades of legacy designs predating modern cyber threats. Increasingly, artificial intelligence is helping adversaries exploit OS vulnerabilities.  To protect embedded systems, Lincoln Laboratory developed an inherently more secure OS called Magnetite. "If Windows and Linux are the familiar workhorses of general-purpose computing, Magnetite is built for the different realities of embedded systems, for which real-time performance matters, resources are tight, and system failure has physical consequences," says Juliana Furgala, principal investigator in the Secure Resilient Systems and Technology Group.  A few components assure Magnetite's security. It is built on top of seL4, a formally verified microkernel (i.e., software core). Formal verification means that mathematical proofs have guaranteed the microkernel's code behaves exactly as intended, eliminating a source of security flaws. On top of this foundation, Magnetite’s OS services — such networking, storage, and communication — are written in Rust. This programming language prevents common memory-corruption bugs that hackers often exploit. Finally, Magnetite configures its services as isolated processes under the principle of "least privilege." This configuration prevents different parts of an embedded system from accessing unnecessary data. If a cyberattack compromises one service, that component can be locked down while critical functions of the system continue running. Free for government use and approved partners, Magnetite is now being integrated into space and flight platforms for the DoW. Looking ahead, the team sees potential to extend the platform to other embedded domains, such as control systems for critical infrastructure. Because Magnetite offers a common, reusable foundation for building specialized mission capabilities, the team is also collaborating with other technical groups across the laboratory to offer Magnetite as an alternative to costly, proprietary operating systems currently in use. In addition to earning an R&D 100 Award, Magnetite was selected as MIT Lincoln Laboratory's Best Invention of 2025. Wafer-scale platform for quantum systems Modern computing systems are increasingly limited not by transistor performance, but by interconnection bottlenecks. Electrical pathways linking densely packed chips are taking up space, slowing data transfer, and generating heat. The problem is especially pronounced in quantum systems, which require bulky coaxial cables to bridge superconducting chips (which must be cryogenically cooled to achieve zero electrical resistance) with room-temperature control electronics. The Quantum Microsystems platform addresses this interconnection challenge, integrating hundreds of superconductor and semiconductor chips into a single, wafer-scale system. The platform combines several innovations. First, an AI decision-tree approach determines the optimal way to route connections between chips across a wafer. After the wafer is tested for defects, a digital lithography process "draws" custom wiring layers between chip locations and around defective circuit components to enable the highest yield possible from the wafer. Chips are then connected using microbump (tiny "bumps" of conductive material used to connect stacked chips) or bumpless techniques that place them extremely close together; a superconducting fabric extends these connections across the wafer to create a unified computing platform, carrying signals at near light speed. Coaxial cables are replaced with integrated, lithographically defined flexible interconnects, significantly reducing cryogenic wiring overhead and system complexity.  The Quantum Microsystems platform is designed to be reworkable, so chiplets can be replaced or upgraded without rebuilding the entire system. The platform enables the design and fabrication of systems ranging from individual and stitched‑reticle architectures to mix‑and‑match multireticle configurations and fully integrated wafer‑scale platforms. The platform's AI engine continuously adapts to process variations and design changes to enable efficient, data-driven microsystem manufacturing.  "By shifting from chip-level scaling to AI-optimized system-level integration, the platform establishes a new paradigm for building ultra-efficient, large-scale computing infrastructure for applications in quantum computing, AI, and high-performance computing," says Rabindra Das, principal investigator in the Quantum-Enabled Computation Group. The technology is designed for transition to government and commercial foundries and may be available for licensing and collaborative development through Lincoln Laboratory’s technology transfer process. Algorithm to cancel 5G interference  As 5G cellular networks have expanded, so has an unintended source of interference. In certain environments, powerful signals emitting from 5G base stations can encroach into frequency bands used by nearby non-5G RF antennas, burying signals for such systems as military radars, aircraft altimeters, satellite ground stations, or radio telescopes.  To cancel this interference, Lincoln Laboratory researchers developed an algorithm that isolates and removes the 5G signal from the affected antenna's signal. Because 5G networks adhere to a published international standard, the canceler can decode the structure of a nearby base station's transmission — and estimate distortion caused by multipath scattering in the environment — well enough to reconstruct a copy of the interfering signal. That reconstructed copy is then subtracted from the incoming data, leaving a clean signal. Unlike traditional interference cancellation approaches like beamforming, the technique does not depend on spatial separation of interfering and desired signals. Moreover, because it removes interference on each individual antenna channel of the receiver, it preserves the antenna resources that may be needed to handle other types of interference, such as jamming. The team validated the algorithm using signals captured over the air from a Nokia 5G base station at Hill Air Force Base. The tests recovered a test radar signal buried by the cellular interference. The signal was restored to within two decibels of its original signal-to-noise ratio, translating to 89 percent preservation of the radar's interference-free detection range.  "While 5G waveforms exhibit complex structure, their generation is governed by global standards that allow our cancellation methodology to generalize across base station radio heads made by a diverse set of vendors," says Binoy Kurien, principal investigator in the Tactical Edge Communications Group.  The DoW is now evaluating the technology for use on multiple platforms. Because the core structure of the 5G waveform is expected to carry into future cellular generations, this approach may also extend to interference from 6G networks as they emerge.
6290eaef59b40da4: Jensen Huang: in the spotlight and out of a job. Nadja Wohlleben/Getty ImagesExtramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.” Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026. The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked. Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose. Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “beauty stratagem.” As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations, I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors. The beauty stratagem of Ancient China “Meiren ji” is one of “Thirty-Six Stratagems,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership. The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience. Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history. In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge. According to the ancient historical text “Wu Yue Chun Qiu,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs. The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu. A 19th-century etching depicting Zheng Dan and Xi Shi. Wikimedia Commons Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery. Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly. A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “Romance of the Three Kingdoms,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature. It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo. The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor. The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “honey trap.” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War. Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu. The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s. Bernard Boursicot and Shi Pei Pu in the dock during an espionage trial in Paris in May 1986. Laurent Maous/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office. Why Jensen Huang is strategically important Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power. Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development. Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers. From Beijing’s perspective, advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition. This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang. However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation. Espionage in the age of AI Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages. What has changed is who controls important strategic resources. In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. Today, approaching a major technology executive could offer access to sensitive technologies. More than 2,000 years ago, a powerful state could lose its advantage through a ruler’s personal weaknesses. Today, political and technological power are distributed differently. But as long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit.
