9ac3f87d0b7ef077: State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years. That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40. The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it. Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “Today oligarchy has won.” As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality, I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second – or third or fourth – homes the very wealthy possess. Taxing the rich at the ballot box Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth. Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed. In Washington state, for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax. Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136, which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87, a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000. And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3. That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000. And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest. The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa. Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “millionaire protection cap.” People visit the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco, on Feb. 21, 2026, months before a ballot initiative that would have introduced such a measure failed to garner enough support. AP Photo/Jeff Chiu State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures, rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged. In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets. And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate. In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes. Washington, D.C., Massachusetts and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023 and 2025, respectively. Taxing additional homes Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences. These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths. Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system, which took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates. New York City rolled out its “pied-à-terre tax” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence. Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences. And on Nov. 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target. However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks about the fiscal year 2027 budget in New York City on May 12, 2026. Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate. Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind. Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property and other assets – many of which are hard to estimate. The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock. Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. Calculating how much tax on real estate someone owes is easy for the authorities to do using annual municipal assessments. What might happen next? Despite Proposition 40’s defeat, it looks like Americans are generally open to taxing wealthy people more – at least when the states do it. In Illinois, where a billionaire governor, JB Pritzer, easily won a third term, another interesting ballot initiative prevailed. More than 75% of voters in Cook County, which includes Chicago and several of its suburbs, approved a nonbinding, advisory referendum asking if Illinois should adopt the “millionaire amendment for property tax relief and education.” It would levy a new surcharge of 3% on incomes over $1 million. While this win did not authorize a new tax, it revealed that support for one would be strong – at least in Chicago and Evanston. Even billionaire Bill Gates has said he believes a “billionaire’s tax” will be necessary. The question is: What kind? 59c5e44d58a3eccd: The first talks between Russia and Ukraine in nine months have concluded. The most positive thing that can be said about the US-mediated meeting in Abu Dhabi was that the dialogue did not break down and the parties seemed to agree to further meetings. There was also at least one tangible result. Russia and Ukraine agreed on a large-scale exchange of prisoners of war, the magnitude of which will be clarified over the coming days. Beyond this, however, there were few signs of progress towards a peace agreement. Despite Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky’s claim that all participants in the negotiation process “genuinely want to achieve a result before 2027”, the most important issues remain unresolved. These include ceasefire terms, the future status of occupied regions and long-term security guarantees for Ukraine. The talks took place against the backdrop of continued fighting on the frontline. Russia’s military currently controls about a fifth of Ukraine, but progress on the battlefield has slowed in 2026 – and has even been reversed – due to Ukrainian successes. With the frontline largely static, Moscow keeps striking Ukrainian cities and energy sites with missiles and drones. In turn, Ukraine has attacked Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure. The Russian military currently controls a fifth of Ukrainian territory. Institute for the Study War According to reports from Abu Dhabi, Ukraine firmly rejected a proposal for it to surrender the entire Donbas region in the east of the country in return for peace. Whether the Russian demand for the Donbas indicates a softening of its claim to the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions remains too early to determine. The deadlock remains on other key issues, too. Russia continues to insist that a restructuring of Europe’s security architecture must be put in place before any ceasefire can take effect, to address what it regards as its legitimate security concerns. On the eve of its full-scale invasion in 2022, Russia demanded the withdrawal of Nato forces from countries that joined the alliance after 1997. These include the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and other eastern European states. If this demand still stands, it is difficult to envisage an end to the war anytime soon. Ukraine, for its part, is bracing itself for another harsh winter. It therefore seeks a ceasefire as the starting point for any serious negotiations on peace. This demand, backed by its European supporters, has so far fallen on deaf ears in the Kremlin. This was evidenced by missile strikes that continued even during the peace talks themselves. The coercive nature of Russia’s strategy was further underlined by the fact that six major electricity substations in central Ukraine were reportedly struck during the night between the two days of negotiations. Perhaps the most important new point of departure for the Abu Dhabi talks was a new initiative by the Trump administration to tie a peace deal to a broader European security framework. US envoy Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, has said this framework would provide security guarantees to Ukraine while also meeting Russian security demands. The details of what such a construction would look like are hidden from the public view. But if the recent stances of the Trump administration are of any guidance, those details are likely to be closer to Russian preferences than Ukrainian ones. In recent weeks, Trump has struck a controversial deal that has allowed Moscow to restore some of its diesel exports, waiving several sanctions in the process. Steve Witkoff, another US presidential envoy, also praised Russian leader Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” in late October. Left in the cold So far, the deep irony seems to be that while the issue of a broader European security architecture is on the table, the European countries supporting Ukraine are denied a place at the negotiating table itself. Even though there were representatives of the EU, Nato, France, Germany, Italy and the UK present in Abu Dhabi, they were not given formal voice in the negotiating process. On the first day of the meeting, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov even sarcastically joked about letting them sit there in their hotels. If the US continues to scale down its military presence in Europe, as Trump has repeatedly hinted it will, responsibility for providing the security guarantees Ukraine will so desperately need after the war will fall largely on the EU and European Nato members. This would again call for giving Europe a voice and presence at the negotiating table, which seems to have been recognised at least by Kushner. After the Abu Dhabi talks concluded, he was reported as saying European partners must be at the table in future rounds. He said he would raise the matter with Putin. Europe’s participation in the talks is not a marginal issue, particularly as the position of the US as an honest broker has become debatable, given the tendency of the Trump administration to side with Russia on essential issues. Trump’s recent remark that Ukraine might “end up with a little bit different shape” after the war suggests this remains the case. The Abu Dhabi meeting has at least revived negotiations between the two warring parties. But it is far from evident that peace has moved any closer. The most contentious issues remain essentially where they were before the parties convened in the Emirates. Bo Petersson receives funding from Malmö University and the Hamrin Foundation.

b5a7a069ea875674: There is a long list of people who have been, or still are, under detention in their own homes around the world.
Many are former heads of state or government. Apart from Najib Razak, we can count Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi and former French president Nicolas Sarkozy among them.
Like Najib, Sarkozy was convicted of a criminal offence. On the other hand, Suu Kyi is being detained for her opposition to the military dictatorship that continues to hold sway in Myanmar.
Another politician who also lived at home but as a prisoner was ex-Argentine president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.
Unlike Malaysia, both Argentina and France already had provisions in their legal systems for home detention when their respective leaders — in this instance de Kirchner and Sarkozy — were sentenced.

In Argentina, the provision for house arrest goes back a long way — all the way back to 1886 when its first National Criminal Code was put in place. There have been several updates — in 1921, 1996 and subsequently in 2008.
According to Argentina.gob.ar, the official portal of the Argentine State, several conditions must be met before a prisoner qualifies for home detention.
He or she must be suffering from a terminal illness, or a malady that “cannot be adequately treated in prison” but does not require hospitalisation.
A person with a disability, making him vulnerable to inhumane or degrading treatment in a prison environment or any person aged over 70 also qualifies. So do pregnant women and caregiving mothers.
At age 72, de Kirchner qualifies on age alone.
In France, house arrest is provided for under Article 142-5 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure.

It states that a person convicted of a criminal offence and sentenced to a year or less in jail can be confined to his home under strict conditions. The prisoner must also show that he does not pose a flight risk.
Sarkozy was sentenced to three years but qualified anyway because two of those three years were suspended.
As far as we know, Najib is neither ill nor pregnant. He does not have any young child to watch over either.
At age 76, former Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Isa Samad is still serving out his six-year prison sentence for corruption. Najib is three years younger than him.
Even if we pick a leaf or two from the Argentine and French playbooks on home detention, Najib does not qualify on any front.

In September, Najib was granted a conditional pardon by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong under which he could serve out the remainder of his six-year sentence in the SRC International case under house arrest.
The condition was that he paid the RM50 million fine. Umno managed to raise the sum and the fine was paid on Nov 6.
Najib is already home to continue serving his sentence, but it is not too late to start thinking about putting in place provisions for house arrest.
Chances are there will be more to come.

4dcaee04b6caac45: The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empowering community members
Originally published on Global Voices
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm. Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon. Used with permission.

Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year. Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September. Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.

Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families. Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment. More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.

Children are among those affected. Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition. Beyond its nutritional consequences, food insecurity can also affect children’s ability to learn and participate in school activities.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), hunger can impair concentration and memory and affect classroom attendance. In February 2026, the organisation reported that only 2.8 percent of primary school pupils in Cameroon received a free hot meal at school, highlighting the limited reach of school lunch programmes.
Conflict, climate-related disasters, agricultural losses and rising staple food prices are among the main drivers of this crisis.
School gardens in action
To combat persistent food insecurity, educators and nonprofit organisations are partnering to teach children how to grow their own food.

In Bamenda, North West region of Cameroon, the Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) runs the ADAPT Programme, which engages 70 pupils from two nursery and primary schools. Created after a survey revealed that few schools had gardens or provided environmental education, the ADAPT Club has established gardens with five sections: nurseries, vegetables, fruit trees, composting and tubers.

Muluh Kelly Vughose, Programme coordinator for ADAPT, says pupils are involved in more than just planting. “Our volunteers, together with the teachers and pupils, designed each garden. Children are also involved in learning basic agricultural skills like plantain propagation and grafting of fruit trees.” The club holds two sessions each week, lasting about two hours.

In the same region, in Nkambe and neighbouring villages, pupils from six primary and two secondary schools are learning agricultural skills through the Smart School Gardens Project, launched by Youth Development Organisation – Yodo Cameroon. Schools have received wheelbarrows, watering cans and compost manure to support the project.

“During the two years of implementation, I have watched these pupils and students care for plants from seed germination until harvest,” says Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s Programme Coordinator. The gardens produce cabbage, huckleberry, carrots and Irish potatoes.

Meanwhile, SUHUCAM’s regenerative school garden programme in the Centre region combines fruit trees, including guava, soursop, orange and papaya, with plantains and produce such as huckleberry, cabbage and waterleaf. Through these activities, pupils are learning techniques such as composting, plant propagation and grafting.

Children are embracing the school gardens with enthusiasm, discovering the importance of food production and sustainability through practical experience. Queeninver Ngwangung, SUHUCAM’s Youth and Advocacy Lead, explains:

“Rather than simply teaching students about sustainable agriculture, food security or climate action, we give them opportunities to practice these concepts,” she said. “Through growing food, managing organic waste and caring for their gardens, we have observed that students have learnt that environmental solutions can begin with everyday actions within their own schools.”

For Amang Mael, a Form Three student, seeing vegetables grow on an abandoned plot behind his school has been particularly exciting. “Since we planted the vegetables, I have been so eager to harvest. We add organic manure to all our crops so they can be healthy.”

Another student, Kouba Princesse, believes the garden can contribute to the fight against hunger. “Now that I know how to grow my own vegetables, I will not have to depend on buying from the market all the time,” she says. Some kids have taken the practice home, where they maintain small gardens and use plastic bottles for drip irrigation during the dry season. Other students also say the experience has sparked an interest in pursuing careers in agriculture.
Supporting community nutrition

In 2025, the ADAPT Club produced approximately 45 kilogrammes of dry compost from biodegradable waste. At the end of each planting cycle, YACA organises a Mini School Garden Market Day, where parents and community members can buy the harvest. “Income gained is reinvested in the next planting cycle,” says Muluh Kelly.

At SUHUCAM, the harvests serve nutritional and educational purposes. Students eat fruits from the gardens, while vegetables are sold to purchase seeds and fund their continued management. Some students take extra produce home to establish household gardens.
After two years with two regenerative school garden cycles, SUHUCAM’s Climate Change and Innovation Club has benefitted thousands of households and planted over 400 trees.

In Nkambe, pupils involved in Yodo Cameroon’s project also sell their harvests to community members at affordable prices. The proceeds have helped schools purchase basic educational materials, including chalk and exercise books. Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s project manager says:

The gardens have become practical outdoor classrooms. Not only are the children learning new agricultural skills, but they are also gaining an appreciation for nature, responsible environmental practices and sustainable resource management.

The nutritional potential of school-based production is also evident in other initiatives. In 2025, an integrated school production programme supported by FAO in Cameroon’s East and South regions established 18 school gardens. The programme produced 236,859 kilogrammes of vegetables, alongside eggs and fish, helping provide weekly healthy meals to 10,833 students. Children, teachers and community members also received training in sustainable agriculture, hygiene and nutrition.

Nkimih Clinton, a researcher at the Institute of Agricultural Research for Development (IRAD), says regenerative practices, such as those deployed in the community gardens, can improve soil health and support sustainable agriculture. Composting, mulching, crop rotation and organic manure, he explains, “can contribute to maintaining the health of pieces of land” for crop production. However, he cautions against expecting small-scale school gardens to eliminate hunger entirely.

Although they may not provide all the food pupils need, they can improve dietary quality by supplying vegetables, legumes and fruits rich in essential vitamins and minerals. “School gardens can be used as a source of production of micro-nutrients to complement basic staples (cassava, maize, rice) provided by parents,” Clinton says.
Challenges to overcome

Despite their benefits, maintaining school gardens remains difficult. Programme coordinators say unpredictable rainfall makes it harder to plan planting activities and sustain crop production. Changing weather conditions can also contribute to pest outbreaks and seed shortages.

Maintaining the gardens during school holidays is another challenge, as pupils are less available to care for the crops. These difficulties can interrupt children’s opportunities to follow the entire production cycle, from planting to harvesting. Expanding the initiatives will therefore require coordinated support from government officials, agricultural research institutions and development partners.
Schools need funding, reliable water supply, farming tools, quality seeds and technical assistance to maintain productive gardens throughout the year.
Government and policy support

Cameroon has previously taken steps to promote environmental education in schools. In 2018, the Ministry of Secondary Education and the Israeli Ambassador to Cameroon launched a Green School campaign that planted 300 trees in 30 schools.

In May 2023, the country launched the second phase of the Classes Vertes project, a three-year initiative developed by FAO in partnership with the Special Council Support Fund for Mutual Assistance (FEICOM) and several government ministries. Targeting 80 schools across the Far North, North, Adamawa, East and South regions, the programme sought to promote vegetable production, fish farming and poultry farming to improve children’s access to nutritious food. It also included tree planting and initiatives to build school canteens, water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities, with an allocated budget of approximately FCFA 722 million (USD 1.2 million).

The government’s commitment to improving children’s access to nutritious food is also reflected in its National School Feeding Strategy for 2025–2030, which aims to expand school meals and strengthen links between schools and local food producers.

Officials hope the program will reach one million learners by 2030. In July 2026, the government, through the Ministry of Basic Education, signed a EUR 3.6 million (USD 4 million) agreement with the World Food Programme (WFP) to expand home-grown school feeding in the Adamawa, East and Far North regions. The 2026–2029 programme is expected to provide nutritious meals to nearly 11,000 children in ten public primary schools while creating market opportunities for 600 smallholder farmers.

Meanwhile, experts believe school gardens can be replicated across Cameroon but stress that their implementation must reflect the country’s different agro-ecological zones. Rather than adopting a uniform approach, schools need solutions suited to their agro-ecological zones.

While school gardens may not independently resolve Cameroon’s food insecurity challenges, they offer opportunities to strengthen children’s nutritional knowledge, promote sustainable agriculture and encourage household food production. Their long-term impact, however, will depend on sustained investment, technical support and policies that enable more schools to establish and maintain these initiatives.
Written by Sandra Tuombouh

a865d7bae4f04a4d: Accurate, up-to-date climate projections are essential for planning decisions that enhance the resilience of power grids, protect public health, maximize agricultural yields, and more. Now, MIT researchers have developed a technique that streamlines the production of fast, trustworthy, and adaptable artificial intelligence models for climate prediction. These specialized AI models, known as climate emulators, can rapidly simulate the effects of human activities onto a future climate, predicting impacts on temperatures or sea level, for example.  Because emulators run in a matter of seconds, scientists use them to efficiently test thousands of varied climate scenarios. This provides more reliable estimates and can identify unexpected outcomes of regional interventions. The MIT researchers developed a training technique that boosts the performance and adaptability of a climate emulator while using only a fraction of the data typically required. This significantly cuts production time for these practical scientific tools. They show that an emulator trained with a much smaller amount of carefully selected synthetic data accurately predicts outcomes of scenarios it did not see during training, while traditional emulators failed to adapt to new situations. “Climate emulators are especially well-suited for modeling policy-relevant scenarios. By using our method to generate optimized training data for an emulator, we can speed up the production of much more reliable emulators, so we can better trust their outputs for making policy decisions,” says Christoher Womack PhD ’26, who is now a postdoc at ETH Zurich and lead author of a paper on this technique. He is joined on the paper by Shahine Bouabid, a postdoc in the MIT Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); Andrei Sokolov, a research scientist in MIT’s Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3); Popat Salunke, a postdoc in CS3; Glenn Flierl, a professor of oceanography in EAPS; Sebastian D. Eastham, an associate professor at Imperial College London; and senior author Noelle E. Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and EAPS, and director of CS3. The research appears this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.  Speedier surrogates Climate scientists typically use earth system models (ESMs) to make long-term projections about how global temperature or precipitation could change in response to varying greenhouse gas emissions. These enormous, physics-based models capture the major components and interactions of the earth’s climate in extreme detail. While powerful, ESMs can take months to run on a cluster of supercomputers — and that’s only to project one possible future climate scenario.  Selin and her collaborators design climate emulators, which are fast AI surrogate models that mimic the behavior of full-scale ESMs. Emulators help scientists test many scenarios, make more accurate forecasts, and explore specific pollutants and regional effects. “Climate emulators can run in just a few seconds, so it really expands what we can do in terms of exploring these future climate scenarios,” Womack says. When scientists design a climate emulator, they often train the AI model using a set of six to eight future scenarios based on realistic future trajectories of emissions. They must run each scenario through a full-scale ESM, making these datasets costly and time-consuming to generate.  The MIT researchers recently found that using realistic future scenarios as training data can lead to underperforming emulators that fail to predict unfamiliar or novel scenarios.  In this work, they developed an algorithm that generates a synthetic dataset of optimized climate scenarios tailored to boost one emulator’s predictive performance. “Our algorithm might generate some weird scenarios which look nothing like a realistic future, but we don’t care so much if the training scenarios are realistic. We are just trying to make the best possible dataset to train an emulator,” Womack says. Importantly, rather than needing to run a full ESM six or eight times to generate training data, a user would only need to run that model once. Tuning the training data  The researchers begin by generating an arbitrary climate scenario using a fast and simple climate model. They test how well their emulator can reproduce the results of that ESM, which gives them a measure of error. Because of the programming technique they used to build the training pipeline, they can iteratively update the training data to increase the emulator’s predictive skill. For instance, the algorithm could increase CO2 emissions dramatically in the year 2050 or rapidly decrease methane emissions in 2037. Then the optimization updates the training data until the emulator’s error level reaches a certain threshold. In the end, rather than resembling realistic scenarios in which emissions follow smooth trajectories, the synthetic data contain rapid variations. “By introducing these high-frequency wiggles and oscillations, our data enable the emulator to extract a lot more information about the overall system,” Womack explains. Their training algorithm outputs these emissions scenarios, which they can use to train an emulator that is more accurate and adaptable. “In the future, we are definitely going to see climates and scenarios we haven’t seen before. If we can simulate these different scenarios more robustly, we can provide more reliable information to the stakeholders who need it,” Selin says. For instance, an emulator trained with their technique can capture the effects of local pollutant control policies that reduce one pollutant while other emissions continue rising. The traditional emulators they evaluated failed this test.   In the long run, Womack hopes this work improves the usefulness of fast and adaptable climate emulators for policy formulation.  “This is such an important piece of the pipeline when it comes to creating useful tools that speak to stakeholder needs. Because the process of training an emulator can takes months or even years, the emulators we have are usually out-of-date. By cutting down that production time, I think this technique will be a game-changer in terms of getting updated tools into the hands of researchers and practitioners,” Selin adds. In the future, the researchers want to test their technique using an emissions scenario generated by a full ESM. They also want to apply it to other types of climate models and explore its effectiveness in broader machine learning and computer vision applications. This research was part of the Bringing Computation to the Climate Challenge (BC3) project and supported by Schmidt Sciences through the MIT Grand Challenges.
474f4a5c982096f4: Since the October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, and during Israel’s now three-year-long retaliation against Gaza, journalism’s traditional commitment to objectivity has been on trial. Reporting on the Israel–Gaza war has been characterised, on social media as much as in the conservative media, as biased one way or the other. Headlines have been parsed and corrected by social media warriors while a war of words between new journalism players and traditional media has been loud and often angry. This clash has emphasised the tension between the objective reporting claimed to be practiced by legacy media and advocacy-oriented reporting that internet journalists believe delivers more truth. In contrast, the Russian military attack on Ukraine has been reported with milder popular criticism. The privileging of one side’s narrative over the other in this conflict appears not to have attracted the same claims of media bias. Numerous studies have shown trust declines when audiences perceive journalism to be advocating for one position over another. In addition, they have a marked preference for news that incorporates a range of views. This led the Centre for Media Transition to examine the way Australian media have framed both international conflicts. Reporting in conflict We sought to understand if particular narratives have been privileged over others and if so, how. It is a normal part of the reporting process for journalists to decide what information to include, omit, emphasise, and contextualise in order to report a story. This framing process allows journalists to make some narratives more dominant and decide what sources are used to support them. On top of framing there is journalistic voice. Despite the best efforts of a reporter to achieve objectivity, this can often be evaluative or subjective. We examined the framing choices made by The Australian, the ABC, 9News.com.au, and The Guardian across the two conflicts when the events being reported were significant in the news cycle. We gauged how each dealt with the dominant narratives emerging from the main parties to the conflicts. We also looked at which voices were given more space, whose stories were personalised or depersonalised, and which contemporary and historical contexts were prioritised or deprioritised. Whose story is being told? Our results show the media outlets across the 2023–2026 events we looked at, shifted their framing between Israeli and Palestinian narratives, depending on events on the ground. Despite the movement in framing, Israeli frames emerged as dominant overall in 49% of surveyed articles against 32% with Palestinian narratives. All the surveyed media outlets engaged closely with Israeli narratives following the October 7 2023 Hamas assault. But as the Palestinian death toll increased and events in Gaza raised alarm bells, the ABC, 9News.com.au, and The Guardian amplified the humanitarian consequences to the Palestinians (Palestinian frames comprised 38%, 27%, and 54% of their respective samples), although the volume of the coverage was smaller. These outlets continued reporting Israeli security concerns as counterclaims while centring Palestinian victimhood until the conflict escalated to involve the US, Iran, Lebanon, and the Gulf states. Only The Australian continued to privilege Israeli perspectives across all surveyed events. The masthead emphasised Israel’s narratives of victimhood, security, and self-defence (71% of the total outlet’s sample adopted Israeli frames as dominant). It also marginalised Palestinian narratives (3% of The Australian’s overall sample used Palestinian frames), including the history of this long and frequently brutal conflict. The Australian was also the only outlet to align pro-Palestinian advocacy in Australia with narratives of antisemitism and social division. It criticised the Greens for the party’s vociferous support for the Palestinians. It also aligned the most radical of pro-Palestinian voices with more moderate ones, particularly around the time of Australia’s recognition of Palestinian statehood in the UN. Ukraine conflict tells a different story In coverage of the Russia–Ukraine war between 2022–2026, our results show a very different use of journalistic framing. We found an asymmetry in engagement with and treatment of the narratives emerging from both sides. Western and Ukrainian narratives were continuously dominant across 67% of the sampled coverage by all four outlets surveyed, and the voices given prominence were overwhelmingly Western and Ukrainian. Russian narratives received almost no interpretive authority. In fact, in the articles we surveyed, 0% engaged with Russian frames as dominant. Indeed, when Russian frames were referenced to understand what Russia still calls a “special military operation” rather than war, it was mostly to disparage them. As a result, historical and geopolitical complexity of post-Soviet foreign policy was significantly downplayed. This includes Russian arguments that NATO’s eastward expansion in Europe was threatening, and Russia did not view NATO as a defence alliance. One strong strain of reporting was that Russian president Vladimir Putin was an irrational actor, and his war on Ukraine indicated a psychological malaise. Another was that Russia was paradoxically threatening yet internally fragile, economically weak yet able to survive global sanctions, unable to conquer Ukraine yet able to wage war against Europe. In this conflict, to a far greater extent than in Israel–Gaza reporting, evaluative journalistic voice was apparent. This portrayed the war through a historical lens of Soviet and Russian expansionism, while references to the controversial Minsk Agreements were largely left unexplored. While source privileging and selective framing are the hallmark of advocacy journalism, this does not necessarily mean a piece of reporting is advocacy. Sometimes, there is broad consensus in support of one side and in opposition to the other – as there is in relation to Russia’s war on Ukraine. In contrast, there are polarised responses around Israel–Gaza, where violations of international humanitarian law against Palestinians and Israel during the Hamas attack were documented. But the journalistic obligation to analyse and engage viewpoints with which journalists may not agree or accept does not simply disappear in the practice of objective journalism. The obligation can disappear in the practice of advocacy journalism such that one side’s interpretation becomes embedded as a default perspective. But the question then becomes whether this is actually journalism. In 2022, Professor Attard was formally banned from entering Russia for what the Kremlin labelled a “Russophobia agenda”. Alena Radina is a Russian citizen.
810cf766812e6045: “If that’s what the law says, then the law is an ass.”

These words are famously associated with Charles Dickens’ 1838 novel, Oliver Twist. However, the expression appeared in print much earlier, in the 1654 play Revenge of Honour: “The law is such an ass.”
It refers to the foolish or rigid application of the law when it defies common sense, humanity or reality.
This remains true today. Our legal ecosystem appears trapped in a time warp.
Consider a recent case in which the High Court rejected a man’s bid to secure Malaysian citizenship for his stateless son, despite DNA tests establishing their biological relationship.
The son has lived in Malaysia since he was three months old, has no birth certificate and has never held citizenship of any country.
Born in Thailand to a Malaysian father and Thai mother, he was ruled ineligible for citizenship by operation of law because his parents could not prove they were legally married when he was born.

The court held that Section 17 of Part III of the Second Schedule of the Federal Constitution applied, treating the child as born out of wedlock. Under that provision, references to the father of an illegitimate child are construed as references to the mother for citizenship purposes.
Unless the law changes, such inflexibility will remain. University students should examine such social issues, particularly cases involving children born out of wedlock.
Politics may prove even more confusing.

Many will recall a former federal minister convicted of murdering his political opponent in the 1980s. His death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment by the Pardons Board, and he was released about eight years later after receiving a royal pardon.

Does this mean society condones murder? Over the years, pardons have been granted to numerous convicted individuals on the merits of their cases, with few questions raised. Can it therefore be argued that society condones their crimes? Politicians and students alike should understand this distinction.

Fast-forward 30 years, and we are debating an unrelated corruption case in which the same discretionary powers of the Federal Territories Pardons Board (FTPB) have been exercised. Yet there are now claims that granting a pardon amounts to condoning corruption.

It is deeply saddening when such arguments come from senior political leaders, including the apparent political theatre surrounding a minister’s decision to step down on the day an individual moves into his home to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.
The granting of pardons by the FTPB, chaired by the King, is part of the legal framework, following a process in which individuals are charged, convicted and sentenced after due process.
The law applies to everyone. Article 8 of the Federal Constitution guarantees equality before the law. Article 8(1) states that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to equal protection.
If the law applies when someone is convicted, it must also apply when a pardon is considered. Should a person be denied the opportunity to seek one because of his standing in society?

Why demand the minutes of an FTPB meeting or suggest something is amiss merely because of the individual involved? To do so without credible evidence implies that not everyone is equal before the law. Could the legal process itself also have been compromised because of the individual’s standing?

Questions have also been raised about the “donations” used to pay the fine, with aspersions cast over their source. These were funds belonging to a political party. Why should anyone dictate how another party uses its funds if they are not members?
We appear blinded by political opportunism, bordering on vengeance. What matters is the spirit of the law.

The recent actions of the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) in Najib Razak’s case have left a bitter aftertaste, regardless of the legal questions surrounding errors in court documents, apparently caused by a lack of scrutiny.
This begs the question: who is the ass here – the law, the drafters, those responsible for scrutinising the documents or those interpreting the discharge order?
Why was the issue raised at the last minute, despite the legal arguments over the wording of the discharge order? Many are now up in arms over the AGC’s position.

This has fuelled interpretations of the motives behind the move. When one institution has two functions – advising the government and acting as public prosecutor – perceptions can easily become tainted.
As a nation, we remain trapped in a political time warp of unholy alliances, racial and religious slurs, and relentless backstabbing, at the expense of more pressing issues.
All parties must stop linking the royal pardon and house-arrest arrangement to condoning corruption. It is demeaning.
A royal decree is a royal decree. We must live with it, while one particular individual gets on with finding another day job.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
01fe3273792f42dd: Ada satu pesona di rak buku ibu yang memikat dan menawan saya iaitu karya Raja Ali Haji, dengan judul Gurindam Dua Belas yang dipercayai dikarang atau tersebar sekitar tahun 1847.

Apa yang menyebabkan saya suka dengan gurindam adalah kerana ia tiada tentu bentuknya. Ia boleh jadi terikat atau tidak. Untuk gurindam dengan bentuk yang terikat, ia terdiri dari dua baris serangkap, mengandungi tiga hingga enam perkataan sebaris dengan rima a-a. Beberapa rangkap berkait akan menjadikan ia satu gagasan atau idea yang boleh dicerna. Sudah tentu Gurindam Dua Belas tersebut memukau saya.

Apabila saya menuliskan novel saya dengan tajuk Koro; salah satu pengikat atau pesona kepada karya ini dibina menerusi gurindam. Koro yang diterbitkan di Indonesia oleh Penerbit Circa pada tahun 2022, dan kemudian diterjemahkan ke bahasa Inggeris oleh Brigitte Bresson, dan diterbitkan oleh Penguin Random House sebagai The Koro Riots (2023) mengisahkan sebuah negara fiksional Republik Hujung Manani yang dilanda penyakit koro iaitu kaum lelakinya mengalami pengecutan alat kelamin mendadak. Sebagai sebuah satira politik, saya cuba mengungkapkan punca korupsi dan kemerosotan moral warga di republik itu dan bagaimana usaha-usaha protagonisnya Negarawan Sejati menegakkan keadilan dan melaksanakan reformasi.

Untuk meyakinkan khalayak akan kewujudan sebuah negara imaginasi ini saya menciptakan lagu kebangsaan, sejarahnya yang pernah ditakluk Perancis, memerikan sosiopolitik dan ekonomi, garis sempadan, dan paling penting negara ini juga memiliki warisan budaya sendiri iaitu gurindam.

Di republik fiksi ini, Gurindam Enam dikenali dan dihafal oleh rakyatnya. Gurindam Enam memerihalkan enam pasal yang mesti diambil kira oleh sesebuah negara untuk kekal merdeka, selamat hala tujunya dan terpelihara dari serangan musuh.

Sudah tentu saya sendiri tidak dapat menjelaskan bagaimanakah ilham atau idea Gurindam Enam ini datang mengalir, melainkan ia terbangun daripada bacaan lampau, perenungan yang bertahun-tahun dahulu disentak oleh karya-karya tradisional yang unggul. Dalam erti kata lain, minda saya secara separuh sedar ketika mengarang Koro dalam tahun 2000 ke 2022 itu melilau dan menerawang di galaksi atau cakerawala fikir yang luas. Ia menjelajah jauh tetapi akhirnya, kembali mendarat di rak buku ibu saya.
Gurindam Enam itu berbunyi begini:
"Dengarkan umat suatu rencana Mengarang kita gundah gulana
Barang gurindam kalau tak kena Sebabnya kita risau kan bangsa
Ini hikmah untuk pemerintah Petua dan syarat memberi faedah
Empat musuh sangat bedebah Ke atas rakyat berbuat payah
Gurindam Pasal Pertama Ada pun negeri hendak selamat Jangan dibiar panjat penjahat
Ada pun penjahat bermacam jenis Ketahui semua umpamakan najis
Ada pun pertama penjilat raja Ikut melanun berbuat dosa
Ada pun perangat ibaratkan kera Menekan rakyat menjarah harta

Barang rakyat jangan dibiar Itulah punca raja pun liar
Barang dinasihat bijak pandai Kalau raja boleh dicanai
Barang yang degil mesti ditangan Tak dapat sanggah mesti dilawan
Gurindam Pasal Ketiga Apabila angkuh kaum agama Harapkan lebai tapi serupa
Apabila lebai serupa anjing Bersama raja menjadi maling

Apabila alim dah jadi baghal Umat tak cegah ditimpa sial

Gurindam Pasal Keempat Khabar diingat perangai Melayu Bangsa beringat menolak candu

Khabar candu bermacam candu Ada ketagih perangai tak malu
Khabar perangai seamat keras Habis pantang semua diganas

Khabar yang ganas usah diulang Perangai yang marah harus dibuang

Kalau ulama lacurkan ilmu Nasib negeri dibidak didadu
Kalau dah Melayu lupa kan ihsan Habis yang kecil sangap ditekan

Inilah akhir gurindam enam pasal yang dikarang oleh Otto Ali pada tahun 1263 Hijrah Nabi hingga dua puluh tiga hari bulan Sya'ban Kamis pukul 05.00 Negeri Hujung Manani."

Di dalam gurindam ini, saya mengungkapkan keseluruhan idea dan gagasan akal budi Melayu, dengan pesan besar bahawa terdapatnya musuh atau ancaman terhadap bangsa yang terdiri dalam bentuk pemerintah yang jahat, dan berpihak kepada yang korup; ulama yang tidak lagi menobatkan kebenaran dan keadilan; rakyat atau warga dilalaikan dengan candu dan madat; serta terakhir kumpulan saudagar kapitalis mementingkan haloba perut berbanding kesejahteraan umat.
Empat kelompok atau golongan yang menentukan arah baik dan buruknya negara ini bukanlah sesuatu yang boleh muncul secara tiba-tiba tentunya. Ia tiba dengan memori berjejak di dalam benak saya.
Enam pasal ingatan dalam gurindam ini dapat direnung dan dicermin kembali dalam pelbagai titah diraja oleh raja-raja Melayu.

Sebagai contoh tuntutan keadilan dan pesan agar raja sentiasa terpandu dinasihati, yang mana dalam konteks zaman moden kita di Malaysia adalah raja berpelembagaan sejajar dengan titah baginda Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan di Istiadat Pengurniaan Darjah Kebesaran, Bintang dan Pingat sempena Hari Keputeraan ke-78 baginda di Istana Besar Seri Menanti pada 14 Jan 2026.

"Rasuah merupakan musuh utama kepada keadilan, amanah dan masa depan negara. Beta amat terperanjat dan kecewa apabila masih wujud pihak yang terus memberikan sokongan kepada individu yang telah disabitkan bersalah atas tuduhan rasuah yang amat besar, seolah-olah perbuatan tersebut boleh diterima dan dimaafkan. Mereka yang masih menyokong penjenayah seperti ini agar segera bermuhasabah diri serta menilai semula pendirian dan kepercayaan masing-masing. Ini kerana sebarang bentuk toleransi atau kompromi terhadap rasuah adalah bertentangan dengan prinsip kebenaran, keadilan serta amanah dan sama sekali tidak boleh diterima dalam sebuah negara yang menjunjung kedaulatan undang-undang."

Tuanku Muhriz berasa khuatir sebarang toleransi dan kelonggaran kepada penjenayah dan jenayah rasuah boleh menjejaskan masa depan negara kita di mana keadilan dilihat tidak lagi dilaksanakan dengan setara, atau terdapat dwistandard antara kelas tertentu.

Baginda tidaklah bersendirian dalam menolak rasuah dan perasuah. Pada 22 Sept 2022 misalnya; Sultan Perak, Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah bertitah, ketika melancarkan buku tulisan M Kamal Hassan bertajuk 'Korupsi dan Kemunafikan Dalam Politik Melayu, Perlunya Disegerakan Transformasi Moral Etika', bahawa rasuah dikenal pasti sebagai salah satu sebab utama yang membantutkan pertumbuhan ekonomi, menghilangkan minat pelaburan asing, meningkatkan kos pentadbiran dan urus niaga, menidakkan rakyat daripada mendapat perkhidmatan, serta mendorong berlakunya ketidakstabilan politik.

Ingatan yang lebih jelas daripada Sultan Nazrin terpancar dalam titah baginda yang lebih mutakhir iaitu pada 2023, ketika Istiadat Menghadap Sembah Taat Setia dan Penganugerahan Darjah Kebesaran Negeri Perak Darul Ridzuan sempena sambutan Ulang Tahun Hari Keputeraan ke-66. Titah Sultan Nazrin lagi rakyat semakin lantang mendedahkan isu rasuah, gigih menolak pemimpin berimej rasuah dan menggunakan jawatan untuk kepentingan diri, atau pemimpin yang mengumpul kekayaan untuk ahli keluarga serta pemimpin yang menjadi instrumen kepada ahli perniagaan.

Saya mengimpikan Gurindam Enam akan menjadi sepertinya Gurindam Dua Belas, sebagai sebuah karya klasik yang bertahan zaman dan dihayati gagasan keseluruhannya seperti mana rakyat Hujung Manani lakukan di dalam novel Koro.

fc712e46e347b6e9: A child struggling to breathe should matter more than a company’s sustainability score.

That should be obvious. Yet every return of regional haze forces an uncomfortable question: are increasingly elaborate environmental, social and governance reporting requirements making the world better, or merely making corporate responsibility look better on paper?
We produce disclosures, establish committees and celebrate compliance. Meanwhile, communities need something simpler: air they can breathe without fearing what it will do to their children.

For Malaysia, the climate and haze crisis must be judged against that basic expectation. A polished sustainability report is not evidence that the people exposed to environmental harm are being protected.
The damage enters our homes
Haze is not merely an unpleasant view from an office window. Smoke contains fine particles, known as PM2.5, that can penetrate deep into the lungs.
Exposure can trigger coughing, wheezing, breathing difficulties and asthma attacks, and increase emergency visits and hospital admissions for respiratory conditions.

Children, older people, expectant mothers and those with existing heart or lung disease face greater risks. Outdoor workers face higher exposure because earning a living may require remaining outside when others can retreat indoors.
Behind these clinical descriptions are ordinary families making difficult decisions.

A parent must decide whether to take leave, arrange childcare or bring a wheezing toddler to a clinic. An older person with breathing problems faces another anxious night. A delivery rider must weigh the need for income against prolonged exposure.
The burden extends beyond treatment. Families can face transport costs, medicine bills and lost work hours. Employers must manage absences. Healthcare facilities must prepare for additional patients.
When schools close, lessons are interrupted and care arrangements become harder. Children lose opportunities to learn, play and socialise.
The United Nations Children’s Fund (Unicef) identifies lost learning and recreational opportunities among the wider consequences associated with wildfire smoke and related disruption.
The injustice is plain: protection should not depend on whether a household can afford filtered air, private treatment or time away from work.
A climate crisis with human fingerprints
Climate conditions can make fires more dangerous, but weather must not become a convenient excuse for preventable damage.

Singapore’s environment ministry has explained that healthy peatlands are wet ecosystems that do not burn spontaneously. Draining peatlands and burning vegetation create fire risks, while prolonged dry conditions can worsen the intensity of fires.
The connection runs both ways. Damaged peatlands become vulnerable to burning, while fires release stored carbon and destroy ecosystems that should help protect the climate.
Preventing haze therefore requires more than extinguishing flames. It requires responsible land management before the burning starts.
The same crisis disrupted transport, trade and tourism and forced school closures. These are historical figures, not estimates for the present episode.
Their significance is that governments and businesses have long had evidence of how destructive uncontrolled fires can become.
Make businesses answerable
ESG reporting should help expose these risks, identify responsibilities and direct resources towards prevention.
But disclosure is a means, not the destination.

A zero burning policy should prompt questions about implementation. Who monitors the land? What happens when fire risks rise? Are suppliers scrutinised? Are prevention teams adequately equipped? Can independent investigators examine what happened?

Malaysian companies with operations abroad should be expected to explain their prevention systems wherever they operate. Geographic distance cannot be a persuasive answer to questions about group oversight.
Equally, accountability requires evidence. A hotspot near a concession is a reason to investigate, not an automatic verdict of guilt.
Authorities must establish where fires occurred, who controlled the land, what duties applied, what preventive measures existed and whether failures contributed to the damage.
Sustainability reports should become documents whose claims can be tested against operational records, independent findings and actual outcomes.
Investors, too, should ask whether returns are being sustained while environmental and health costs fall on people outside the balance sheet.
Replace reassurance with consequences
Malaysia needs a public response that begins before air quality deteriorates.

Authorities should publish clear warnings, practical school and workplace protocols, and arrangements to protect vulnerable communities. Health services should prepare for increased demand, rather than leave families navigating another emergency alone.
Regional cooperation must become operational. The Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution already provides for prevention, monitoring, information exchange and mutual assistance.
Governments should demonstrate how these commitments translate into timely action. What about the penalties for those nations that fail to abide by these agreements?
Regulators must turn disclosures into investigations where warranted, and findings into enforcement. Boards must take responsibility for prevention across their operations and supply chains.
Investors and lenders must demand evidence that commitments are implemented.

Where wrongdoing is proven, those responsible must face meaningful penalties and pay for the damage caused, with board members held accountable wherever the evidence and applicable law establish personal liability.
Yet what accountability, if any, have we seen at board level in Malaysia over haze linked to operations in Kalimantan?

If Malaysian companies operate there, their directors must answer legitimate questions about oversight, fire prevention and whether their sustainability commitments are being honoured beyond our borders.
The costs must not simply remain with families, healthcare workers and taxpayers.
For Malaysia and our neighbours, the demand should be unequivocal: prevent the fires, establish responsibility, enforce the law and ensure those found liable pay for the damage.
Do not ask communities choking on haze to applaud another sustainability report. Show them what changed because of it.
Fewer fires. Fewer hospital visits. Fewer school closures. Cleaner air.
That is the ESG scorecard that matters.

d417f905ed65d8ee: A Salvadoran Army soldier stands guard at a camp in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Oct. 31, 2026. Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty ImagesOn Nov. 10, 2026, El Salvador President Nayib Bukele posted footage of attack helicopters firing on a compound near Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince. He had earlier requested, via a social media post in Haitian Creole, the address of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, one of Haiti’s most powerful criminal organizations. Bukele subsequently claimed the operation, conducted with Haitian police, had demolished Joseph’s residence and gang headquarters. As many as 20 people were killed, although Joseph was reportedly absent. The attack comes amid a flurry of anti-gang operations in Haiti. On Nov. 6, Mathias Saintil, head of the “Boston” gang in Cité Soleil, was killed in a drone strike by a Haitian special task force, prompting Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé to declare on the social media platform X “one less gang leader.” Erik Prince, founder of the private military firm Vectus Global, responded: “Nice shot.” As an expert on organized crime in Latin America and the Caribbean, I believe these operations mark both a dramatic escalation in Haiti’s fight against organized crime and the first overseas test of Bukele’s security model. The intervention is drawing support from some regional leaders and pro-Bukele networks, even as concerns grow over civilian casualties and whether military gains can translate into lasting security. Rescue mission or military offensive? El Salvador already had a limited presence in Haiti as one of six countries contributing personnel to the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force, or GSF. The force was authorized in 2025 to help Haitian authorities reclaim cities and streets from violent gangs that control swathes of the impoverished nation. But it remains severely understaffed and has struggled to translate military operations into lasting territorial gains. Then, in an Oct. 18 gang ambush, four Salvadoran aviation technicians attached to the Gang Suppression Force disappeared. Their burned vehicle was recovered, but their fate remains uncertain. Either way, Bukele used the incident to justify expanding El Salvador’s military presence in Haiti. Within weeks he had sent roughly 2,500 troops, along with armored vehicles and attack helicopters, in what he initially called a rescue mission. They joined an already crowded battlefield. Haiti’s police and army operate alongside the GSF, authorized but not commanded by the United Nations. The Haitian task force involved in operations against Saintil also works with former Blackwater CEO Prince’s Vectus Global, while vigilante groups patrol contested neighborhoods. Dozens of armed gangs associated with the gang coalition Viv Ansanm control large parts of Port-au-Prince and operate beyond the capital. Special forces from El Salvador ride in a Gang Suppression Force truck in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Oct 23, 2026. Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty Images The Gang Suppression Force was authorized by the U.N. Security Council to deploy up to 5,550 personnel, and it currently has roughly 2,000 on the ground. Most of the Salvadoran troops now in Haiti operate outside its command. Haitian Prime Minister Fils-Aimé insists that Haiti directs the operations. Yet neither government has publicly disclosed the agreement specifying Salvadoran authority, rules of engagement or the deployment’s duration. Without a published deployment agreement, the chain of command and rules for authorizing strikes remain unclear to the public. Despite President Donald Trump’s support for Bukele, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has distanced Washington from the Salvadoran offensive, saying the U.S. was “not actively involved.” He warned that poor coordination could lead to friendly fire, while U.S. diplomats formally protested the risks to multinational troops and civilian personnel. Salvadoran authorities dispute American allegations that their gunfire struck the U.S. embassy and endangered multinational troops. They also questioned the credibility of the top U.S. diplomat in Haiti. Uncertain rules of engagement Haiti’s security crisis is dire. In recent years, organized violence has reached levels associated with armed conflict. Almost 6,000 people were killed in 2025, and more than 4,000 in the first nine months of 2026. Nearly 1.5 million Haitians have been displaced as of August 2026, and expanded offensives and gang reprisals could drive more from their homes. An independent legal assessment by the Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights classifies fighting between Haitian forces and the Viv Ansanm coalition as a noninternational armed conflict, a legal category that includes civil wars. The International Committee of the Red Cross has separately warned of the risks to civilians, urging all sides to respect international law. The distinction matters because the rules on lethal force are different in war and policing. Both require civilians to be protected. But in an armed conflict, members of armed groups with combat roles can be targeted even when they pose no immediate threat. In a police operation, simply being suspected of gang membership is not enough to justify killing someone – lethal force is generally allowed only when necessary to protect lives. Of particular concern is the growing use of explosive drones and helicopter attacks in residential areas. At least 1,243 people were killed in 141 drone operations between March 2025 and January 2026, including at least 60 people reportedly unconnected to gangs, 17 of them children. These operations predated the Salvadoran escalation but demonstrate the risks of using explosive weapons in populated areas. At the same time, overlapping mandates for foreign troops and private military contractors could complicate investigations into civilian casualties and allegations of unlawful attacks. Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé and Col. Jose Figueroa of the Salvadoran Army address the media about security operations on Nov. 3, 2026. Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty Images Exporting the Bukele model Some Haitians, exhausted by insecurity, welcome the international intervention. Crowds have cheered Salvadoran soldiers, waving sticks and chanting Bukele’s name. A prominent Haitian human rights advocate supported the deployment while warning that residents of gang-controlled neighborhoods are not necessarily gang members. Bukele promotes the offensive through videos of troops and airstrikes amplified by Salvadoran officials and pro-government influencers. Messages in Haitian Creole and Spanish that portray the strikes as victories against gangs closely resemble the government’s widely circulated footage of mass arrests and prison transfers in El Salvador. Under Bukele, who came to power in 2019, homicides in El Salvador have plummeted, boosting a belief in parts of South America and the Caribbean that an iron fist approach to gang violence is worth the associated cost to human rights. Indeed, security hardliners across Latin America have pointed to El Salvador’s falling homicide rate to justify similar crackdowns. Dominican President Luis Abinader has endorsed the intervention and confirmed logistical and intelligence cooperation. Yet the Salvadoran model has relied on emergency powers and mass incarceration. Around 1.7% of Salvadorans are imprisoned – by far the highest rate in the world. Haiti presents greater operational challenges. According to the U.N. Office for Drugs and Crime, gangs hold extensive territory, possess heavy weapons and maintain connections to political and commercial networks. Haitian institutions are weaker, and children are widely recruited into armed groups from a young age. Sustaining territorial gains would require functioning police and courts, along with protection for residents after foreign troops leave. The expanded Salvadoran presence in Haiti also carries political risks for both governments. Bukele is seeking a third term in February 2027, following constitutional changes that removed presidential term limits. Salvadoran military casualties could stir criticism at home and pressure him to escalate, particularly with the four Salvadoran technicians whose disappearance prompted the rescue mission still missing. For his part in Haiti, Fils-Aimé has publicly backed the offensive ahead of Haiti’s elections, scheduled for July and October 2027. Civilian casualties or failure to sustain gains could undermine his own government’s credibility. Beyond military operations The deployment may foreshadow wider regional security arrangements. El Salvador belongs to the U.S.-backed Shield of the Americas, a coalition launched by Trump in March 2026 to expand military cooperation against drug cartels and other transnational criminal groups. The Salvadoran operation in Haiti does not formally fall under that initiative, whose 15 signatories have pledged closer security cooperation. But such partnerships could allow regional governments to deploy forces with American logistical support while limiting direct U.S. military involvement. Although the Salvadoran operation is the latest high-profile example, I have seen similar cycles working in Haiti since the 2000s. U.N. peacekeepers and Haitian police cleared parts of Cité Soleil between 2007 and 2009, contributing to a decline in kidnappings but failing to deliver lasting security. The U.N. mission later introduced cholera following the 2010 earthquake, killing more than 9,000 people and prompting an eventual apology from the U.N. Gangs endure because their economic networks survive military offensives. They profit from kidnappings and illicit trade while controlling access to key roads and markets. Removing leaders can weaken organizations without ending these revenue streams. While the current Salvadoran offensive may deliver short-term security gains, sustaining them will depend on Haitian institutions maintaining control of recovered territory. Bukele’s intervention is now an overseas test of a security model with considerable political appeal. But its consequences will ultimately be measured by whether Haitians are safer when foreign forces depart. Robert Muggah is the co-founder of the Igarapé Institute, and a principal of the SecDev Group. He also advises governments, private companies, non-profits and international organizations such as the United Nations, the IMF and the World Bank.
d5227a85f3e0f37b: I’m not an expert on highways or infrastructure, but I drive a lot because of necessity, and also because I like being on the road. I’ve done at least 1.5 million kilometres in my life, and I have a bad back and knees and rather diminished retirement savings because of it.

Malaysia has an amazing network of highways and federal and state roads. They’re the literal backbone of our national development, and having put in around 200,000km of driving abroad, I can say that our roads aren’t too bad at all.

There’s a caveat though. For the money we’ve spent on them, they should’ve been much better. I’d give an A minus for the overall national road architecture, though only a C for that in Kuala Lumpur, and another C for the design, construction and maintenance of these roads, especially the newer ones. And it’s an E and very close to an F for the lack of transparency about their ownership, costs and toll charges.

The financial incentives of owning a highway concession, as well as the benefits of political patronage (read: corruption) in parcelling out these concessions to favoured parties leaves quite a sour taste. Our great highways and networks come at too high a cost borne by taxpayers, and especially highway users. It need not have been this way.

My biggest concern is that Malaysia is turning into a car society the same way as the US. Cars seem to be the answer to everything. We’re building out our cities, towns, suburbia, villages, industrial parks, public highways and private turnpikes as if motor vehicles are the only means of transport.

Kuala Lumpur’s downtown area is reasonably compact, but try walking from one point to another. The route would either be inconvenient, dangerous or downright impossible. Everywhere we go, cars get priority and pedestrians and non-motorised cyclists are left to fend for themselves.

We’ve convinced ourselves that our climate is too hot, humid and rainy, and that our roads are too dangerous and inconvenient. There is certainly some truth there, but mostly because the original designs of our living spaces didn’t provide much in the way of alternatives to motorised vehicles.
Addicted to cars

Unfortunately, the manufacture, import and ownership of cars and the taxes and duties due on them makes them too critical to our economy, one of the largest car markets in the region. Cars are a drug we’re unable or unwilling to give up because of the negative impact on our economic health. So, we take higher and higher doses of this “drug” and convince ourselves it is vital to our existence and prosperity.

But the world is changing. Car ownership, especially in mature economies, is not growing by leaps and bounds any more. Certainly, electric vehicles (EVs) are addressing some of the problems associated with them such as pollution, use of environmentally destructive fossil fuels etc. But even if we end up with EVs replacing all fossil fuel vehicles, we still wouldn't have made much progress.

Part of our love affair is certainly psychological. Many Malaysians, myself included, are first-time car owners. Car ownership is an important milestone in our life, often a sign that we’ve reached a certain level of success in life. We haven’t become inured to cars the way many in the more developed societies have. You can take our cars away, as the saying goes, only from our cold dead hands.

But our children and grandchildren aren’t heading that way. Populations are increasingly being concentrated in massive urban conurbations, with such population growth, often caused by urban migration, leading to huge megalopolises such as Jakarta, Mexico City, Lagos etc as well as to the older ones such as Tokyo and Los Angeles.

The coming generations will not have the same love affair with cars as we do. Cars will be just a means of getting from A to B and no longer an important milestone in their life. Many cities are increasingly building out alternative urban transport systems such as light rail, monorail and trams, as well as simpler solutions such as climate-controlled walkways and corridors to cater to the needs of their growing but less car-fixated population.
What lies ahead

Technology recognises this change. The latest self-driving EVs aren’t meant to help us drive our cars better, but rather to create a market where we can just dial up a driverless car that can take us to wherever we need to go without having to own such cars or deal with their drivers.
It will create a new business of the car-as-a-service, with cars used on subscription or rented from manufacturers the same way as computer software has been for quite a while.

We risk leaving behind a vast network of expensive but underutilised roads as well as unfit, unhealthy people whose lives are overly spent in the air-conditioned comforts of their houses, cars, offices or shopping malls.

The focus on cars also means rail is often neglected. We’re just beginning to start operating the East Coast Railway Link (ECRL), and even then both its reason for existence and its long-term sustainability are in doubt. Rail can’t win against cars because of the huge capital costs and timeframes involved, unless the government is willing to tip the scales in its favour through incentives and disincentives to the rakyat.

We have over 5,000km of expressways, over half of which are tolled, and the rest would likely end up being tolled too. The appetite to build more highways, driven by politics and surging demand caused by escalating car ownership, will just mean that more toll highways with E designations and fancy names will appear.

It’s not all or nothing. We can both benefit from the economics of car ownership and prepare for a future where cars are not that critical to our lives any more. We need the political will to make alternatives to just having more and more cars and more and more roads for them to drive on.
